questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman undergoes CT of the abdomen, and the radiologist notes the spleen in the left upper quadrant. In relation to the surrounding organs, where is the spleen normally located?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior to the stomach, anterior to the left kidney, lateral to the pancreas

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior to the stomach, posterior to the left kidney, medial to the pancreas

choices.label: C
choices.text: Posterior to the stomach, anterior to the left kidney, lateral to the pancreas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Posterior to the stomach, anterior to the left kidney, medial to the pancreas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Posterior to the stomach, posterior to the left kidney, medial to the pancreas

explanation.summary: The spleen sits in the left upper quadrant, posterior to the stomach, anterior to the left kidney, and lateral to the pancreas.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen lies almost entirely intraperitoneally in the left upper quadrant, shielded by ribs 9 to 11. It sits behind (posterior to) the stomach and just beneath the diaphragm, with the tail of the pancreas reaching its hilum, so the spleen is lateral to the pancreas and anterior to the left kidney.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The spleen is posterior, not anterior, to the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The spleen is anterior to the left kidney and lateral (not medial) to the pancreas, and it lies posterior to the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen is lateral, not medial, to the pancreas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen is anterior to the left kidney and lateral to the pancreas, not posterior and medial.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man undergoes splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision ruptures his spleen. His physician emphasizes vaccination and counsels him that, without a spleen, he is at increased risk for severe infection. Infection with which of the following types of organisms is he now most susceptible to?

explanation.summary: People can live without a spleen but become especially susceptible to severe infections from encapsulated bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in the absence of the spleen, individuals become more susceptible to severe infections, especially from encapsulated bacteria. The white pulp and marginal zone are critical for tagging and clearing encapsulated organisms such as pneumococci, so their loss leaves the patient vulnerable to these bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dermatophyte fungal infections are not the classic post-splenectomy risk described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spleen's protective role highlighted in the brick is against encapsulated bacteria, not enveloped viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The heightened risk is specifically from encapsulated organisms, not non-encapsulated gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Helminth infections are not the characteristic susceptibility that follows loss of the spleen.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease comes in with pain and a full feeling in his upper abdomen for one week. Physical exam shows an enlarged spleen, and his hematocrit and red blood cell count are mildly reduced. Which of the following best explains why his spleen is enlarged?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bacterial abscess within the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased splenic removal of damaged red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neoplastic infiltration of the spleen by lymphocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Storage of an excess number of platelets

explanation.summary: In hemolytic diseases such as sickle cell disease, the spleen enlarges because it must remove large numbers of damaged red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: One function of the spleen is to remove damaged RBCs from the circulation. In sickle cell disease the abnormal RBCs are continually damaged and must be cleared, putting the spleen into overload and causing it to enlarge. This matches his mildly reduced hematocrit and RBC count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no fever or other evidence of a splenic abscess in this hemolytic presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neoplastic lymphocyte infiltration occurs in some leukemias, but nothing in this sickle cell presentation points to a malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Portal hypertension causes congestive splenomegaly through venous backpressure, but this patient has a hemolytic condition, not liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic enlargement tends to lower the platelet count by storing platelets; excess platelet storage is not the cause of splenomegaly here.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A histologic section of the splenic red pulp shows extravascular spaces packed with tissue macrophages that are engulfing aged and damaged red blood cells. Which of the following structures is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Germinal center of a lymphoid follicle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marginal zone at the follicle border

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sinusoids of the red pulp

explanation.summary: The splenic cords are extravascular spaces of the red pulp containing macrophages that phagocytose old or damaged RBCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic cords (cords of Billroth) are extravascular structures that contain tissue macrophages responsible for phagocytosing damaged or old RBCs, along with reticular cells and connective tissue. During open circulation, RBCs percolate through these cords where the macrophages remove defective cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The germinal center is at the center of a white pulp follicle and contains activated B cells, not RBC-clearing macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The marginal zone lies in the white pulp at the border of the follicle and screens blood, rather than serving as the main RBC-phagocytosing space.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is a white pulp region rich in T cells, not the site of RBC phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sinusoids are the leaky vessels that return healthy RBCs to the circulation; the macrophage-filled extravascular space is the cords.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: In the splenic red pulp, older and inflexible red blood cells cannot squeeze through the narrow slit-like openings between the elongated endothelial cells lining the sinusoids, whereas flexible cells pass through and re-enter the circulation. Which of the following cells creates this physical filter?

explanation.summary: Stave cells are the elongated endothelial cells that line splenic sinusoids and form slit-like openings testing RBC flexibility.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sinusoids of the red pulp are lined by elongated endothelial cells called stave cells, surrounded by reticular fibers in a barrel-like fashion to create small slit-like openings. Only flexible (nonsenescent) RBCs can pass through these slits; older, inflexible cells are retained and phagocytosed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Megakaryocytes produce platelets and are not part of the sinusoidal filter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reticular cells make the reticular (collagen III) fibers that surround the stave cells, but the elongated endothelial cells forming the slits are the stave cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T lymphocytes reside in the white pulp and have no role in the physical RBC filter of the red pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue macrophages phagocytose the retained damaged RBCs, but they do not form the slit-like filter of the sinusoid wall.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: The splenic vein exits the spleen at the hilum and courses toward the liver, where it merges with the superior mesenteric vein. This union forms which of the following vessels?

explanation.summary: The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The splenic vein courses toward the liver and ends by merging with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein, which then carries blood toward the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The celiac trunk is an artery arising from the aorta, not a vein formed by this merger.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava; they are not formed at this junction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The inferior mesenteric vein is a separate tributary of the portal system, not the vessel formed by this union.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The inferior vena cava is a systemic vein and is not formed by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is found on exam to have an enlarged spleen. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his splenomegaly?

explanation.summary: In portal hypertension, elevated portal vein pressure backs up into the splenic vein and produces congestive splenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Portal hypertension, an increase in portal vein pressure due to hepatic disease such as cirrhosis, causes increased backpressure transmitted to the splenic vein. This raised pressure may cause fluid to leak from the splenic vein and lead to splenic enlargement, termed congestive splenomegaly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A splenic artery aneurysm is an arterial outpouching and is not the mechanism of enlargement in cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clearing encapsulated bacteria is an immune function of the spleen and does not explain congestive enlargement from cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neoplastic lymphocyte infiltration occurs in some leukemias, but this patient's liver disease drives venous congestion instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thoracic duct obstruction affects lymph drainage systemically and is not the described cause of congestive splenomegaly.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: The splenic artery travels within the splenorenal ligament and enters the spleen at the hilum. This artery is a direct branch of which of the following vessels?

explanation.summary: The splenic artery is a branch of the celiac artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The splenic artery is a branch of the celiac artery, which is the first major arterial branch of the abdominal aorta. It travels in the splenorenal ligament to enter the spleen at the hilum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The splenic artery arises from the celiac artery, not directly from the aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut and is unrelated to the splenic artery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The left renal artery supplies the kidney and does not give rise to the splenic artery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The superior mesenteric artery is a separate branch of the aorta supplying the midgut, not the origin of the splenic artery.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A histologic section of the splenic white pulp shows a sheath of lymphocytes wrapped around a central arteriole. Which of the following cell types predominates in this region?

explanation.summary: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) surrounds the central arteriole and is rich in T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sheath of lymphocytes around the central arteriole is the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS), which mostly contains T cells. T cells are delivered to the PALS by the central arteriole and are activated against invading antigens or neoplastic cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes predominate in the splenic follicles, not in the sheath directly surrounding the central arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages are found in the splenic cords and marginal zone, not as the predominant cell of the PALS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are not the resident lymphocyte population of the white pulp PALS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells derive from activated B cells and are not the defining population of the PALS.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with streptococcal pneumonia. In his spleen, the antibody-producing cells that help fight this encapsulated organism reside mainly in which of the following regions?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Splenic cords of the red pulp

choices.label: C
choices.text: Splenic follicles of the white pulp

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic sinusoids of the red pulp

explanation.summary: B cells that produce antibodies reside in the splenic follicles of the white pulp.
explanation.whyCorrect: The periphery of the white pulp contains numerous splenic follicles largely made up of B lymphocytes, which are responsible for producing antibodies as part of the immune response. These follicles (including the germinal center, mantle zone, and marginal zone) are the main site of the antibody response against encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococci.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is rich in T cells, not the antibody-producing B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The splenic cords are red pulp structures involved in phagocytosing damaged RBCs, not antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sinusoids are blood vessels that return healthy RBCs to the circulation, not sites of B-cell antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trabeculae are fibrous septa carrying vessels; they do not house antibody-producing cells.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with massive splenomegaly is found to have a low platelet count, although her bone marrow shows normal numbers of megakaryocytes. Which of the following best explains her low platelet count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A congenital defect in platelet granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilution of platelets by intravenous fluids

explanation.summary: The spleen stores platelets, so an enlarged spleen sequesters platelets and can lower the circulating platelet count.
explanation.whyCorrect: One function of the spleen is to store platelets, and the brick notes that enlargement of the spleen can lower the platelet count. In splenomegaly, a greater fraction of platelets is sequestered in the spleen, reducing the number in circulation even when marrow production is normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A granule defect affects platelet function, not the circulating platelet count driven here by splenic sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Her marrow shows normal megakaryocytes, so decreased production is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no indication of fluid dilution, and this would not selectively explain splenomegaly-associated thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased platelet production would tend to raise, not lower, the platelet count.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: The splenic capsule is a layer of dense fibroelastic tissue that can contract to discharge stored red blood cells into the circulation and stretch to accommodate incoming blood. Which of the following cells within the capsule provides this contractile function?

explanation.summary: The splenic capsule contains contractile cells called myofibroblasts that let it discharge stored RBCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The splenic capsule is dense fibroelastic tissue that also contains contractile cells called myofibroblasts. Their contraction discharges RBCs into the circulation, and the capsule can also stretch to accommodate incoming blood cells as needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dendritic cells participate in the immune response in the marginal zone, not in capsular contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reticular cells produce the reticular fibers of the red pulp; they do not provide the capsule's contractile function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stave cells are the elongated endothelial cells lining the splenic sinusoids, not contractile cells of the capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue macrophages phagocytose damaged RBCs in the cords rather than contracting the capsule.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A pathologist compares the spleen of a second-trimester fetus with that of a healthy adult. Which of the following functions is performed by the fetal spleen but is taken over by another organ after birth?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filtration of aged red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Storage of T and B lymphocytes

explanation.summary: The fetal spleen is a hematopoietic organ until the bone marrow is fully developed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the spleen's general functions, hematopoiesis is unique to fetal life: the fetal spleen makes blood cells before the bone marrow has fully developed. After that, blood cell production shifts to the marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Removal of blood-borne organisms continues in the adult; loss of the spleen raises the risk of severe infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Filtering out aged and damaged red blood cells is a lifelong function of the red pulp, not one that is handed off after birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen continues to store platelets throughout life; enlargement can lower the circulating platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Storage of T and B lymphocytes persists in the adult spleen, which acts as a secondary lymphoid organ.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to describe the dimensions of the normal adult spleen, the body's largest lymphovascular organ. Which of the following best approximates its normal length and weight?

explanation.summary: The normal adult spleen is about 11 cm long and weighs roughly 150 g.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen measures approximately 11 cm (4.3 in) in length and weighs about 150 g (5.3 oz), making it the body's largest lymphovascular organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These values are far too small and would represent a markedly atrophic organ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 20-cm, 400-g spleen represents splenomegaly rather than normal size.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 30-cm, 900-g organ would be massive splenomegaly, as seen with infiltrative or congestive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These values exceed even massive splenomegaly and do not describe a normal spleen.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is stabbed in the left upper quadrant. The trauma surgeon notes that the spleen normally lies deep to a portion of the bony thorax, which shields it anteriorly. Which of the following ribs normally overlie and protect the spleen?

explanation.summary: Ribs 9 to 11 shield the spleen anteriorly in the left upper quadrant.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen sits almost entirely intraperitoneally in the left upper quadrant and is shielded anteriorly by ribs 9 to 11 as well as by its dense fibroelastic capsule.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribs 1 to 3 are at the thoracic inlet and are nowhere near the left upper quadrant viscera.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ribs 2 to 4 lie over the upper thorax, far above the spleen's position beneath the left hemidiaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ribs 4 to 6 are still too superior; the spleen lies behind the lower left ribs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribs 5 to 7 overlie thoracic structures superior to the level at which the spleen lies.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A histologic section of spleen shows fibrous septa extending inward from the capsule at the hilum, carrying branches of the splenic artery, splenic vein, lymphatics, and nerves into the splenic pulp. These septa are best termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: Capsular septa that carry vessels and nerves into the splenic parenchyma are the trabeculae.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the hilum the capsule forms septa that pierce the splenic pulp; these are the trabeculae, and they convey branches of the splenic artery, vein, lymphatics, and nerves into the parenchyma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The marginal zone is a lymphoid region at the edge of a splenic follicle, not a connective tissue septum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is a cuff of T cells in the white pulp surrounding a central arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reticular fibers are fine collagen III fibers that band the sinusoids; they do not carry vessels into the organ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic cords are extravascular spaces of the red pulp filled with macrophages, not fibrous septa from the capsule.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: During a splenectomy, a surgeon divides the peritoneal ligament that runs from the greater curvature of the stomach to the spleen. Which of the following structures must she expect to encounter within this ligament?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inferior mesenteric vein and left colic artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Left renal artery and left renal vein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels

explanation.summary: The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the spleen and, besides attaching the two organs, contains the short gastric arteries and veins and the left gastroepiploic artery and vein, all branches or tributaries of the splenic vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The inferior mesenteric vein and left colic artery serve the hindgut and do not run between stomach and spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The renal vessels run in the retroperitoneum to the kidney and are not contents of a gastric peritoneal ligament.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The splenic artery and vein travel in the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament, not the gastrosplenic ligament.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The superior mesenteric vessels supply the midgut from the root of the mesentery, away from the gastrosplenic ligament.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A surgeon dividing the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament during a splenectomy takes care not to injure a non-vascular structure that lies within it alongside the splenic artery and vein. Which structure is she protecting?

explanation.summary: The splenorenal ligament contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.
explanation.whyCorrect: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the left kidney and contains the splenic artery and vein as well as the tail of the pancreas, which lies adjacent to the splenic hilum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The duodenojejunal flexure is located at the ligament of Treitz in the midline, not at the splenic hilum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The head of the pancreas lies to the right, cradled by the duodenum, far from the splenic hilum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The left adrenal gland sits retroperitoneally atop the left kidney and is not a content of this ligament.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The left ureter descends retroperitoneally from the renal pelvis toward the bladder, outside this ligament.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Lymph emerging from the splenic hilum first enters splenic lymph nodes located near the tail of the pancreas. Which of the following describes the remainder of this lymph's route back to the bloodstream?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Celiac nodes, then the cisterna chyli, then the thoracic duct, then the left subclavian vein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Celiac nodes, then the right lymphatic duct, then the right subclavian vein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inguinal nodes, then the cisterna chyli, then the thoracic duct, then the left subclavian vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mesenteric nodes, then the cisterna chyli, then the right lymphatic duct, then the right subclavian vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Para-aortic nodes, then the thoracic duct, then the right subclavian vein

explanation.summary: Splenic lymph passes through celiac nodes and the cisterna chyli to the thoracic duct and the left subclavian vein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymph draining the spleen goes from the splenic nodes at the hilum to the celiac nodes, then to the cisterna chyli and the thoracic duct, which empties into the left subclavian vein to rejoin the systemic circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The right lymphatic duct drains the right head, neck, upper limb, and thorax, not the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and perineum and have no role in draining upper abdominal viscera.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesenteric nodes drain the intestines, and the splenic lymph ultimately reaches the thoracic duct rather than the right lymphatic duct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thoracic duct terminates on the left side, at the left subclavian vein, not the right.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Autonomic fibers reach the spleen by traveling along its arterial branches, forming a plexus at the splenic hilum. From which of the following do these sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers arise?

explanation.summary: The spleen is innervated by the celiac plexus via the splenic plexus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autonomic innervation to the spleen travels along its vessels from the celiac plexus and includes both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. At the hilum these fibers form the splenic plexus, which follows the splenic arterial branches into the organ.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The inferior hypogastric plexus innervates pelvic viscera such as the bladder and rectum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pulmonary plexus lies at the lung hila within the thorax and supplies the airways and lung vasculature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The renal plexus accompanies the renal arteries to the kidneys rather than to the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The superior mesenteric plexus follows the superior mesenteric artery to supply midgut derivatives.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: To emphasize the scale of red cell filtration in the spleen, a hematology lecturer quotes the volume of blood that passes through the organ in a single day. Approximately what volume is this?

explanation.summary: Roughly 350 L of blood traverse the spleen each day.
explanation.whyCorrect: Approximately 350 L of blood pass through the spleen per day, which conveys how extensively circulating red cells are screened by the red pulp.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 3.5 L approximates a person's total circulating blood volume, not daily splenic throughput.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 15 L would represent only a few passes of the entire blood volume through the organ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 35 L is an order of magnitude below the volume that actually perfuses the spleen daily.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 3,500 L overstates splenic flow by an order of magnitude.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Red blood cells reach the splenic sinusoids by either open or closed circulation. Which of the following correctly describes closed circulation in the spleen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood drains into the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath before entering the sinusoids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood empties into the splenic cords before entering the sinusoids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blood enters the germinal centers before entering the sinusoids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood flows through the trabeculae before entering the sinusoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blood passes from the capillaries directly into the sinusoids, bypassing the cords

explanation.summary: In closed circulation, capillary blood enters the sinusoids directly without traversing the splenic cords.
explanation.whyCorrect: Closed circulation moves blood from the capillaries straight into the sinusoids, bypassing the splenic cords. Open circulation is the alternative route, in which blood first empties into the cords and red cells must then squeeze into the sinusoids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is a T-cell region of white pulp and is not a conduit for red cell flow into sinusoids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emptying into the cords first is the defining feature of open circulation, not closed circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Germinal centers house activated B cells in the follicles and are not part of the red cell circulatory route.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trabeculae are connective tissue septa that carry vessels; blood does not percolate through the septa themselves.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Over its lifespan a red blood cell accumulates defects in its cell membrane that render it susceptible to destruction by macrophages in the splenic cords. Approximately how long does a normal red blood cell circulate?

explanation.summary: Red blood cells normally survive about 120 days before splenic removal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red blood cells have a lifespan of roughly 120 days. Over that time membrane defects accumulate, making the cells inflexible and susceptible to phagocytosis by macrophages in the splenic cords.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Seven days is far shorter than the normal red cell lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thirty days would imply a markedly shortened survival, as occurs in hemolytic states.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sixty days is only about half the normal circulating lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A year greatly exceeds the survival of a normal red blood cell.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Tissue macrophages in the splenic cords phagocytose aged and damaged red blood cells. In addition to clearing these cells and removing intracellular inclusions, which of the following do these macrophages do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Form the slit-like openings through which red cells pass

choices.label: B
choices.text: Produce antibodies directed against encapsulated organisms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recycle iron captured from the destroyed red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secrete the collagen III fibers that band the sinusoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Store platelets for later release into the circulation

explanation.summary: Splenic cord macrophages remove inclusions from red cells and recycle their iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Besides phagocytosing damaged or old red cells, the macrophages of the splenic cords remove intracellular particles called inclusions and recycle the iron captured from the red cells they destroy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The slit-like openings of the sinusoids are formed by stave cells banded by reticular fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody production is carried out by B cells in the splenic follicles and marginal zone, not by cord macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticular fibers of collagen III are made by reticular cells, not by macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet storage is a property of the spleen as an organ, not a phagocytic function of cord macrophages.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of the splenic red pulp shows fibers encircling the elongated endothelial cells of a sinusoid in a barrel-like fashion, leaving narrow slits between them. These fibers are best characterized as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collagen I laid down by myofibroblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collagen III produced by reticular cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collagen IV produced by endothelial cells

explanation.summary: Reticular fibers banding the splenic sinusoids are collagen III made by reticular cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stave cells lining the splenic sinuses are surrounded by reticular fibers, which are collagen III produced by reticular cells. Their barrel-hoop arrangement creates the small slit-like openings that only flexible red cells can traverse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Myofibroblasts are the contractile cells of the splenic capsule; they are not the source of the sinusoidal fiber bands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fibers banding the sinusoids are described as reticular collagen III, not a basement membrane collagen made by endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stave cells are the elongated endothelial cells themselves; the encircling fibers are laid down around them by reticular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrin is a product of coagulation within the vessel lumen and does not form the structural bands of the sinusoid wall.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has chronic anemia with ongoing destruction of red blood cells, and her spleen is enlarged on examination. Which of the following conditions is a classic cause of this pattern of splenic enlargement?

explanation.summary: Hemolytic anemias such as hereditary spherocytosis enlarge the spleen because damaged red cells must be cleared.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen enlarges in many types of hemolytic anemia, in which damaged red blood cells must be removed from the circulation. This is particularly notable in the thalassemias, sickle cell disease, and hereditary spherocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia of chronic disease arises from disordered iron handling and reduced production rather than hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aplastic anemia reflects failure of marrow production, so there is no increased splenic red cell clearance driving enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency anemia results from inadequate iron for hemoglobin synthesis, not from accelerated red cell destruction in the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs red cell maturation in the marrow rather than causing the splenic overload of hemolysis.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A flexible red blood cell squeezes through a slit between stave cells and enters a splenic sinusoid. Which of the following vessels does it enter next on its way back to the systemic circulation?

explanation.summary: Red cells leaving the sinusoids drain into tributaries of the trabecular veins before reaching the splenic vein.
explanation.whyCorrect: After red cells enter the sinusoids by either open or closed circulation, they return to the circulation via tributaries of the trabecular veins and ultimately leave the organ through the splenic vein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The central arteriole delivers blood and lymphocytes into the white pulp; it is an inflow vessel, not an outflow route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The inferior mesenteric vein drains hindgut structures and is not part of the intrasplenic outflow pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The left gastroepiploic vein likewise drains the stomach rather than carrying blood out of the splenic pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The short gastric veins run in the gastrosplenic ligament and drain the stomach into the splenic vein.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A section of splenic white pulp shows a spherical follicle with concentric zones. The innermost zone contains B cells that have been activated in response to antigen. Which of the following is this zone?

explanation.summary: The germinal center sits at the center of the splenic follicle and holds activated B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic follicles have concentric zones like those of lymph nodes. The germinal center lies at the center of the follicle and contains activated B cells, with resting B cells and the antigen-screening region arranged around it.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The mantle zone lies just outside the germinal center and is an area of resting B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The marginal zone is the outermost follicular region, at the margin between the follicle and the PALS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath surrounds the central arteriole and is rich in T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic cords are red pulp structures filled with macrophages, not zones of the follicle.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Within the splenic white pulp, one region lies outside the mantle zone and forms the interface between the B-cell-containing follicle and the T-cell-containing periarteriolar lymphoid sheath, permitting antigen exchange between them. Which region is this?

explanation.summary: The marginal zone is the link between the splenic follicle and the PALS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The marginal zone lies outside the mantle zone, at the margin between the follicle and the PALS. It serves as an important link between the B-cell-containing follicles and the T-cell-containing PALS and allows antigen exchange between the follicle and PALS and between red and white pulp.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The germinal center is the innermost follicular zone and holds activated B cells rather than forming an interface.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mantle zone sits between the germinal center and the marginal zone and contains resting B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sinusoids are the leaky red pulp vessels through which flexible red cells return to the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trabeculae are fibrous septa carrying vessels and nerves; they are not a lymphoid interface zone.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: In the marginal zone of the splenic white pulp, one cell type captures blood-borne antigens and presents them to T cells residing in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath. Which of the following cells performs this role?

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells in the marginal zone trap antigen for presentation to PALS T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The outer ring of the marginal zone contains reticular fibroblasts, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Of these, the dendritic cells trap antigens and present them to the T cells in the PALS, linking blood screening to the T-cell response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Megakaryocytes are marrow cells that give rise to platelets and are not resident antigen-presenting cells of the marginal zone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myofibroblasts reside in the splenic capsule and contract it to discharge stored red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticular fibroblasts are present in the outer ring but function as structural support rather than trapping antigen for T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stave cells are the elongated endothelial cells of the red pulp sinusoids and serve a filtering, not antigen-presenting, role.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops pneumococcal bacteremia. Which of the following best describes how the marginal zone of his spleen defends against this encapsulated organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B cells rapidly produce antibodies that tag the organism for adjacent macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Megakaryocytes release platelets that aggregate around the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Myofibroblasts contract the capsule to expel the organism into the sinusoids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticular cells deposit collagen III fibers that wall off the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stave cells trap the organism in the slits between sinusoidal endothelial cells

explanation.summary: Marginal zone B cells make antibodies that opsonize encapsulated bacteria for neighboring macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: A key immunologic function of the marginal zone is that B cells there rapidly produce antibodies that tag pathogens for destruction by the adjacent macrophages, a response that is especially important against encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococci.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The spleen stores platelets, but platelet release is not the marginal zone's defense against encapsulated organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Capsular myofibroblast contraction discharges stored red cells into the circulation and has no antimicrobial role.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticular cells produce the collagen III fibers that support the sinusoids; they do not wall off bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sinusoidal slits formed by stave cells filter inflexible red cells in the red pulp; they are not the antibacterial mechanism of the marginal zone.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: T cells populating the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath are delivered there from the bloodstream, where they are then activated against invading antigens or neoplastic cells. Which of the following structures delivers them?

explanation.summary: The central arteriole delivers T cells from the blood into the PALS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PALS is a sheath of T cells wrapped around a central arteriole. The T cells are delivered to the PALS from the blood by that central arteriole, where they are then activated in response to invading antigens or nonself neoplastic cells and remove the invaders from the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic capillaries drain lymph from the hilum toward the splenic nodes; they do not seed the PALS with T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenic cords are extravascular red pulp spaces housing macrophages that phagocytose damaged red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sinusoids return filtered red cells to the circulation in the red pulp rather than delivering T cells to white pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trabecular veins carry blood out of the spleen and are part of the outflow, not the inflow, pathway.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: Although most splenic immune activity takes place in the white pulp, the red pulp also participates in the immune response. Which of the following immune activities occurs within the red pulp?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated B cells proliferate within the center of a lymphoid follicle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigen is exchanged at the margin between a follicle and the PALS

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigen is presented within a sheath of lymphocytes around a central arteriole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages induce differentiation of T cells circulating through the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resting B cells are held in a zone immediately surrounding the germinal center

explanation.summary: Red pulp macrophages and natural killer cells contribute to immunity, including driving T-cell differentiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophages and natural killer cells in the red pulp interact with white pulp cells and assist in eradicating pathogens from the blood, and red pulp macrophages can induce differentiation of T cells that circulate through the spleen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Proliferation of activated B cells occurs in the germinal center of a white pulp follicle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigen exchange at the follicle-PALS interface occurs in the marginal zone of the white pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lymphocyte sheath around a central arteriole describes the PALS, which lies in the white pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Holding resting B cells is the role of the mantle zone, a white pulp follicular zone.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with a chronic hemolytic anemia is found on routine examination to have an enlarged spleen. He plays several recreational sports and asks whether he should change anything. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop all sports and aerobic exercise permanently

explanation.summary: An enlarged spleen is more easily injured, so contact sports should be avoided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with splenomegaly are advised to refrain from contact sports, because an enlarged spleen extends beyond the protection of the rib cage and is more likely to be damaged during such activities. Treating the underlying hemolytic process should reduce splenic size.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron supplementation does not address the splenic enlargement caused by clearing damaged red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenectomy is not the first response to splenomegaly; managing the underlying disorder should shrink the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dietary protein restriction has no bearing on splenic size or on the risk of splenic injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blanket avoidance of aerobic exercise is unnecessary; the concern is blunt trauma to the enlarged organ.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: The spleen lies almost entirely intraperitoneally, yet one region of its surface is not invested by peritoneum because vessels, lymphatics, and nerves enter and leave there. Which region is this?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The visceral surface overlying the stomach

explanation.summary: The splenic hilum, where blood flows into and out of the spleen, is not covered by peritoneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hilum is the site where blood flows into and out of the spleen and is the region not covered by peritoneum. It is also where the capsule forms the trabeculae that carry the vessels, lymphatics, and nerves into the pulp.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The diaphragmatic surface is smooth and convex where it contacts the diaphragm and ribcage and is peritonealized.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The inferior pole carries peritoneum like the rest of the organ; the vessels enter centrally at the hilum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The superior border is part of the peritonealized surface of the organ rather than the vascular entry point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The visceral surface is irregular and concave where it contacts abdominal viscera, but it is still covered by peritoneum away from the hilum.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A pathologist examining a splenic biopsy comments that she cannot cleanly isolate red pulp from white pulp in the specimen. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both pulps are replaced by adipose tissue in adults

choices.label: B
choices.text: Red pulp is present only at the hilum

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two pulps are separated only by the trabeculae

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two tissues are intermingled throughout the parenchyma

choices.label: E
choices.text: White pulp is confined to the fibroelastic capsule

explanation.summary: Red and white pulp are intermingled, so a biopsy cannot separate them.
explanation.whyCorrect: The splenic parenchyma consists of red pulp and white pulp, named for their gross appearance, and the two tissues are intermingled. Because of this, a biopsy of the spleen makes it difficult to isolate one from the other, and red pulp is seen interdigitating with white pulp histologically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adult spleen retains functioning red and white pulp and is not replaced by fat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red pulp makes up most of the splenic parenchyma rather than being restricted to the hilum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trabeculae are vessel-carrying septa; they do not act as a boundary that neatly divides the two pulps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: White pulp lies within the parenchyma around the central arterioles, not within the capsule.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use disorder presents with abdominal fullness. Examination reveals ascites, spider angiomata, and a spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show thrombocytopenia and elevated liver function tests. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his splenomegaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of amyloid protein within the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Entrapment of rigid, sickled red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased splenic vein pressure from portal hypertension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infiltration of the spleen by leukemic cells

explanation.summary: Chronic liver disease causes splenomegaly through vascular congestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cirrhosis raises portal venous pressure due to scarring within the liver. This is transmitted downstream to the splenic vein, increasing splenic pressure and blood volume, which enlarges the spleen. Sequestration of platelets in the congested spleen explains the thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid deposition causes splenomegaly through infiltration and is seen in amyloidosis, not as a consequence of cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cell entrapment causes splenomegaly in hemolytic anemias such as sickle cell disease, not cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs when the bone marrow fails, as in myelofibrosis, and is not the driver here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infiltration by leukemic cells is a mechanism seen in hematopoietic malignancy, not in a patient whose findings point to chronic liver disease.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 28-year-old restrained driver is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He reports left upper quadrant pain. His heart rate is 88/min and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. He is alert with strong pulses and intact breath sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: B
choices.text: CT scan of the abdomen with contrast

explanation.summary: In a hemodynamically stable trauma patient, CT with contrast is the preferred test to evaluate suspected splenic injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has LUQ pain after blunt trauma but is hemodynamically stable with a normal heart rate and blood pressure. A stable patient can safely undergo CT with contrast, which best defines the presence and extent of splenic injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bedside ultrasound is used to screen hemodynamically unstable patients, where time is critical, not stable patients who can tolerate CT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Embolization or splenectomy are treatments considered after imaging identifies the injury, not the initial step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exploratory laparotomy is reserved for unstable patients or those with peritoneal signs; this stable patient first needs imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plain abdominal x-rays are not useful for diagnosing splenic abnormalities.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman underwent surgical splenectomy after a splenic rupture during a motor vehicle accident. Vaccination against which of the following types of pathogens is most important in this patient?

explanation.summary: Asplenic patients are at greatest risk from encapsulated bacteria and must be vaccinated against them.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen produces antibodies that opsonize encapsulated organisms for immune destruction. Without a spleen, patients are at high risk of overwhelming sepsis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type B, and Neisseria meningitidis, so vaccination against these encapsulated bacteria is essential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vaccination against DNA viruses is not the priority in asplenia; the key threat is encapsulated bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fungal infection is a concern mainly in immunocompromised hosts and is not the priority vaccination in asplenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonencapsulated bacteria are effectively cleared without splenic opsonization of a capsule, so they are far less dangerous than encapsulated organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parasites are not the encapsulated organisms that the spleen specifically defends against.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: During an anatomy dissection, a medical student identifies a small, red nodule adjacent to the stomach. Cross-section of the nodule demonstrates both red pulp and white pulp. Which of the following is the identified nodule?

explanation.summary: An accessory spleen is the most common congenital splenic anomaly and contains red and white pulp like normal spleen.
explanation.whyCorrect: An accessory spleen is extra, healthy splenic tissue separate from the main body of the spleen. It is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, and, like a normal spleen, it is composed of white pulp and red pulp.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The adrenal gland shows a cortex and medulla, not the red and white pulp characteristic of splenic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A kidney is not this small and shows a cortex and medulla on cross-section rather than splenic pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lymph node has a cortex and medulla with follicles, not red and white splenic pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pancreas has a tan/beige gross and cross-sectional appearance and lacks red and white pulp.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with sickle cell disease has a peripheral blood smear showing red blood cells containing small, dark, round nuclear remnants (Howell-Jolly bodies). This finding most strongly indicates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: The spleen is absent or not functioning properly

choices.label: D
choices.text: The spleen is enlarged and hyperfunctioning from hemolysis

explanation.summary: Howell-Jolly bodies signal that the spleen is absent or nonfunctional.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen normally removes red blood cells with abnormalities, including retained nuclear DNA remnants. When Howell-Jolly bodies persist in the circulation, it indicates the spleen is absent or not functioning, as occurs in sickle cell disease after splenic auto-infarction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extramedullary hematopoiesis reflects blood cell production outside the marrow and does not by itself explain Howell-Jolly bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency produces microcytic, hypochromic cells, not Howell-Jolly bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A hyperfunctioning spleen would clear these DNA remnants; their presence indicates loss of splenic function, not overactivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, not this splenic-clearance finding.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing splenomegaly is found to have anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia. Her bone marrow biopsy is normal and shows no infiltrating cells. Which of the following best explains her low blood counts?

explanation.summary: Hypersplenism is an overactive spleen that removes blood cells faster than normal, causing cytopenias.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypersplenism is a complication of splenomegaly in which an overactive spleen removes blood cells faster than normal, decreasing one or more cell lines. This produces anemia, thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk, and leukopenia with infection risk, consistent with a normal marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The marrow biopsy is normal with no infiltrating cells, excluding marrow infiltration as the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemodilution does not selectively lower all three cell lines through active destruction in an enlarged spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic changes rather than pancytopenia driven by an enlarged, overactive spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood loss would cause anemia but does not explain the simultaneous drop in platelets and white cells.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with infective endocarditis develops fever, left upper quadrant pain, and leukocytosis. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a fluid-filled collection within an enlarged spleen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A splenic abscess typically arises from bacteremia complicating infective endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic abscesses are intrasplenic pus collections that most often result from systemic bacteremia, frequently as a complication of infective endocarditis. Patients present with fever, LUQ pain, splenomegaly, and leukocytosis, and CT is the gold standard showing an intrasplenic collection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An accessory spleen is asymptomatic normal splenic tissue, not a febrile fluid collection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amyloid infiltration enlarges the spleen through protein deposition and does not produce fever and a pus collection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Physiologic asplenia is a small, nonfunctional spleen from auto-infarction and does not present with an abscess cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic rupture follows trauma and presents with hemorrhage and hemodynamic changes, not an infectious pus collection.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated after a bicycle crash in which he struck his left flank. He has left upper quadrant tenderness and reports pain in his left shoulder, though the shoulder itself is uninjured. Which of the following best explains the shoulder pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fractured left clavicle with local tenderness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute myocardial infarction of the inferior wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Left lower lobe pneumonia with fever and cough

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rotator cuff muscle strain with painful abduction

explanation.summary: Left shoulder pain after blunt trauma (Kehr sign) suggests splenic rupture with diaphragmatic irritation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with splenic rupture may present with referred pain to the left shoulder, known as the Kehr sign, caused by irritation of the diaphragm from intra-abdominal blood. In a patient with LUQ tenderness after left flank trauma, this strongly suggests splenic injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A clavicle fracture would produce local bony tenderness and deformity, not referred pain with LUQ tenderness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myocardial infarction is not the expected cause of shoulder pain in a young trauma patient with abdominal findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pneumonia would present with respiratory symptoms and fever rather than post-traumatic LUQ tenderness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rotator cuff strain causes pain with shoulder movement, not referred pain linked to abdominal trauma.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease undergoes abdominal CT for unrelated pain. The scan reveals a small, shrunken, calcified spleen. Which of the following processes best explains this appearance?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior surgical removal of the spleen

explanation.summary: In sickle cell disease, recurrent vaso-occlusive crises cause splenic auto-infarction and physiologic asplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickle cell disease initially causes splenomegaly as sickled RBCs are trapped, but over time repeated vaso-occlusive crises form small clots in the splenic blood supply. The organ shrinks to a fibrous, calcified, nonfunctional remnant through auto-infarction, producing physiologic asplenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid infiltration enlarges the spleen with protein deposits rather than shrinking it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Congenital absence would mean no spleen is present, whereas a small calcified remnant is visualized here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis enlarges the spleen through blood cell production, the opposite of this shrunken appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The imaging shows a shrunken, calcified spleen that is still present, not an absent, surgically removed organ.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. Her heart rate is 130/min and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. Her abdomen is distended, and a bedside ultrasound shows free intra-abdominal fluid. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CT scan of the abdomen with contrast

explanation.summary: A hemodynamically unstable trauma patient with free intra-abdominal fluid needs urgent operative exploration.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hemodynamically unstable patients, time is critical. A bedside ultrasound that detects intra-abdominal fluid indicates ongoing splenic bleeding, and a diagnostic laparotomy should be performed urgently to control the hemorrhage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CT with contrast is reserved for stable patients; an unstable patient cannot safely wait for it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endovascular embolization is used in more stable patients with slow bleeding, not in acute hemodynamic instability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Observation is appropriate only for stable patients without peritoneal signs, not for shock with free fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Outpatient follow-up is dangerous in a patient who is actively bleeding and in shock.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with primary myelofibrosis is found to have massive splenomegaly. His bone marrow is fibrotic and cannot adequately produce blood cells. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his splenic enlargement?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Entrapment of rigid red blood cells from hemolysis

explanation.summary: When the marrow fails, blood cell production shifts to the spleen, causing extramedullary hematopoiesis and splenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: In disease states such as primary myelofibrosis, the bone marrow cannot adequately synthesize blood cells, so hematopoiesis (especially RBC production) occurs in the spleen. This extramedullary hematopoiesis enlarges the organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid deposition is a form of infiltration seen in amyloidosis, not the driver in myelofibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red cell entrapment causes splenomegaly in hemolytic anemias, not in marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An intrasplenic abscess is a localized infection, not the mechanism of diffuse enlargement in myelofibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal hypertension enlarges the spleen through vascular congestion and would present with liver disease findings, not marrow fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is suspected of having an enlarged spleen on physical examination. Her physician wants to confirm the finding and accurately measure the size of the spleen. Which of the following is the best test for this purpose?

explanation.summary: Abdominal ultrasound is the best test for measuring the size of the spleen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenomegaly can be confirmed with imaging, and abdominal ultrasound is the best test for measuring the size of the spleen. It is less useful than CT/MRI for internal detail, but for sizing the organ it is the modality of choice.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plain abdominal x-rays are not useful for diagnosing or sizing splenic abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Angiography assesses blood vessels and is not used to measure the size of the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic biopsy carries bleeding risk and is reserved for unknown diagnoses, not for measuring size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A PET scan evaluates metabolic activity and is not the standard tool for measuring spleen size.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for several weeks of vague left-sided abdominal fullness. He is examined supine and then in the right lateral decubitus position with his neck, hips, and knees flexed, and the area beneath the left costal margin is palpated with and without inspiration. Which of the following findings on this examination would confirm splenomegaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spleen palpable more than 2 cm below the left costal margin

choices.label: B
choices.text: A spleen that is not palpable while the patient lies supine

choices.label: C
choices.text: A spleen tip appreciated only at the end of expiration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dullness to percussion beneath the right costal margin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tenderness over the left lower ribs with deep palpation

explanation.summary: Finding the spleen more than 2 cm below the left costal margin on palpation indicates splenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Examination of the abdomen on inspiration is critical, with the patient palpated in both the supine and right lateral decubitus positions and the neck, hips, and knees flexed. The spleen is palpated under the left costal margin with and without inspiration, and a spleen felt more than 2 cm below that margin indicates splenomegaly. Tip enlargement of 1-2 cm is not sufficient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The spleen is palpated in both supine and right lateral decubitus positions, so absence of a supine finding alone does not exclude or confirm enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The maneuver depends on inspiration, which pushes the spleen downward; a tip felt at end-expiration is not the defining criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant, so right-sided percussion findings do not address splenic size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rib tenderness reflects chest wall or rib injury rather than the size of the underlying spleen.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with three weeks of abdominal distension and right upper quadrant discomfort. Examination shows tender hepatomegaly, ascites, and a spleen palpable below the left costal margin. Doppler imaging demonstrates thrombosis of the hepatic veins. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Hepatic vein obstruction, commonly called Budd-Chiari syndrome, raises splenic pressure and causes splenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hepatic vein drains the liver, so hepatic vein obstruction increases pressure upstream and is transmitted to the spleen, enlarging it. This obstruction is most often due to hepatic vein thrombosis or blockage by a tumor, and any such obstruction of blood flow is commonly referred to as Budd-Chiari syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiphospholipid syndrome is a thrombotic state that predisposes to splenic abscess; it names the tendency to clot rather than this hepatic venous syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Felty syndrome is splenomegaly occurring with rheumatoid arthritis, not a consequence of hepatic vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary myelofibrosis enlarges the spleen through extramedullary hematopoiesis and would not produce tender hepatomegaly with hepatic vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic artery thrombosis is an uncommon cause of an absent or nonfunctioning spleen, not of congestive hepatomegaly with ascites.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man reports progressive shortness of breath. Examination shows distended neck veins, rales on pulmonary auscultation, hepatojugular reflux, and pitting edema of both lower extremities. His spleen is palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Which of the following best explains his splenomegaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Congestive heart failure raising systemic venous pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Entrapment of rigid red blood cells within the spleen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis from bone marrow failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperplasia of splenic lymphocytes from chronic infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infiltration of the spleen by deposited amyloid protein

explanation.summary: Right heart failure raises venous pressure diffusely and traps blood in the spleen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congestive heart failure, especially right heart failure, leads to diffusely increased venous pressure, which results in increased blood volume trapped within the spleen. The accompanying findings of pitting edema, jugular venous distension, shortness of breath, rales, and hepatojugular reflux identify this vascular congestion as the mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cell entrapment enlarges the spleen in hemolytic anemias with rigid cells, not in venous congestion from heart failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs when the marrow cannot make blood cells, as in myelofibrosis, which this presentation does not suggest.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased splenic immune activity follows infection or autoimmune disease and is accompanied by fever and leukocytosis rather than right-sided heart failure signs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amyloid deposition enlarges the spleen by infiltration in amyloidosis and does not produce edema, rales, and hepatojugular reflux.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis is evaluated for recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Her spleen is palpable below the left costal margin, and her white blood cell count is 2,100/mm3 with neutropenia. Which of the following terms best describes this combination of findings?

explanation.summary: Rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly is named Felty syndrome, an autoimmune cause of increased splenic immune activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune disorders cause the spleen to mount an increased immune response with hyperplasia of its resident lymphocytes and macrophages, enlarging the organ. Among the autoimmune causes listed for splenomegaly are lupus, rheumatoid arthritis (Felty syndrome), and autoimmune hemolytic anemias, and the low white count with recurrent infection fits the syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiphospholipid syndrome is a thrombotic state listed as a risk factor for splenic abscess, not a rheumatoid arthritis-associated splenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Budd-Chiari syndrome refers to obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, an entirely vascular cause of splenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gaucher disease is a congenital lipid storage disease that enlarges the spleen by deposition of lipid, unrelated to rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Niemann-Pick disease is a congenital disorder with sphingomyelin deposition in the spleen, not an autoimmune syndrome.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college wrestler is diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. He feels much better after two weeks and asks when he can return to the mat. His spleen remains palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He may return to wrestling after one additional week of rest

choices.label: B
choices.text: He may return to wrestling as soon as his fever resolves

choices.label: C
choices.text: He should avoid contact sports for 6 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: He should begin prophylactic penicillin and return to wrestling now

choices.label: E
choices.text: He should undergo elective splenectomy before returning to wrestling

explanation.summary: Splenomegaly from mononucleosis warrants avoiding contact sports for 6 months to lower rupture risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic rupture can occur if a patient with splenomegaly sustains splenic trauma, so an enlarged spleen must be protected from abdominal trauma. A patient with splenomegaly due to infectious mononucleosis should avoid contact sports for 6 months to lower the risk of splenic rupture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A week of rest is far short of the interval needed for the enlarged spleen to be protected from traumatic rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Resolution of fever does not mean the spleen has returned to normal size, and the enlarged spleen remains vulnerable to rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotic prophylaxis addresses infection risk in asplenia and does nothing to protect an enlarged spleen from traumatic rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is performed for trauma, malignancy, severe infection, or massive symptomatic enlargement, not to allow an athlete to resume sport.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man developed splenomegaly three weeks ago during acute infectious mononucleosis. His physician explains that his spleen is more likely to rupture after minor trauma than the chronically enlarged spleen of a patient with long-standing cirrhosis. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute enlargement is accompanied by severe thrombocytopenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recent splenic infarction has weakened the parenchyma

choices.label: C
choices.text: The acutely enlarged spleen lies entirely below the rib cage

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fibrous capsule has not had time to thicken

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular congestion is always greater in acute enlargement

explanation.summary: An acutely enlarged spleen ruptures more easily because its capsule has not yet thickened.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenomegaly is itself a risk factor for rupture. An acutely enlarged spleen, meaning enlargement present less than one month, is more likely to rupture from trauma than a chronically enlarged spleen, because the fibrous capsule has not had time to thicken.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration is a feature of chronic congestive splenomegaly and is not what makes the acutely enlarged capsule fragile.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenic infarction is the process seen with repeated vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease, not a feature of acute infectious splenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spleen sits in the left upper quadrant under the ribs, and this rib coverage is what makes it vulnerable to chest wall injury in either case.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased splenic immune activity, not greater vascular congestion, drives enlargement in mononucleosis, and congestion is not the stated reason for the rupture risk.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and abdominal distension. Imaging shows hepatosplenomegaly, and tissue analysis reveals accumulation of glycosaminoglycans within the spleen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Splenic accumulation of glycosaminoglycans identifies a congenital mucopolysaccharidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infiltration of the spleen by protein, lipid, or carbohydrate deposits is one mechanism of splenomegaly. Among these congenital and acquired storage conditions, the mucopolysaccharidoses are the congenital disorders in which glycosaminoglycans accumulate, producing organomegaly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Amyloidosis is an acquired disease in which amyloid protein, not glycosaminoglycan, is deposited within the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gaucher disease is a congenital lipid storage disease, so the accumulated material is lipid rather than glycosaminoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Niemann-Pick disease is a congenital disorder characterized by accumulation of sphingomyelin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sarcoidosis enlarges the spleen through infiltration by granulomatous cells, not by stored carbohydrate.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is evaluated for cough and fatigue. Chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and a lymph node biopsy demonstrates noncaseating granulomas. Abdominal imaging shows an enlarged spleen. Which of the following best explains the splenic enlargement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of amyloid protein within the red pulp

choices.label: B
choices.text: Entrapment of rigid, nondeformable red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis replacing the red pulp

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased splenic vein pressure from portal hypertension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infiltration of the spleen by granulomatous cells

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis enlarges the spleen by infiltrating it with granulomatous cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infiltration of the spleen by cells or protein deposits is a recognized mechanism of splenomegaly, and granulomatous cells seen in sarcoidosis are one such infiltrating population. Hilar lymphadenopathy with noncaseating granulomas identifies sarcoidosis as the underlying process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid deposition causes infiltrative splenomegaly in amyloidosis, which does not produce noncaseating granulomas in hilar nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cell entrapment explains splenomegaly in hemolytic anemias with rigid cells, such as sickle cell anemia and hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs when the marrow cannot adequately synthesize blood cells, as in myelofibrosis or leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased splenic vein pressure follows chronic liver disease, which this patient's findings do not suggest.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman reports lifelong episodes of jaundice, fatigue, and dark urine. Examination shows pallor, scleral icterus, tachycardia, and a spleen palpable below the left costal margin. Her peripheral blood smear shows numerous spherocytes. Which of the following best explains her splenomegaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulomatous infiltration of the splenic white pulp

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperplasia of lymphocytes from chronic infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Portal hypertension caused by hepatic scarring

choices.label: D
choices.text: Storage of abnormal lipid within splenic macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trapping of rigid, nondeformable red blood cells

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis enlarges the spleen because rigid red cells are trapped within it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some hemolytic anemias, including sickle cell anemia, the major thalassemias, and hereditary spherocytosis, are characterized by rigid, nondeformable red blood cells that become trapped within the spleen, leading to splenomegaly. The accompanying anemia, pallor, fatigue, tachycardia, jaundice, and hemoglobinuria are the expected signs and symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulomatous infiltration is the mechanism in sarcoidosis, which does not cause a lifelong hemolytic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte hyperplasia reflects increased splenic immune activity from infection or autoimmune disease, with fever and leukocytosis rather than hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal hypertension causes congestive splenomegaly in chronic liver disease and would not produce spherocytes on the smear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipid storage within splenic macrophages occurs in congenital storage diseases such as Gaucher disease, not in spherocytosis.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man returns for follow-up 6 weeks after splenectomy performed for traumatic splenic rupture. He feels well and has no fever, pain, or bleeding. His white blood cell count is 14,500/mm3 and his platelet count is 690,000/mm3. Which of the following best explains these laboratory findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells normally stored in the spleen remain in the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Development of a myeloproliferative disorder of the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marrow response to an unrecognized infection of the surgical wound

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ongoing occult bleeding from the splenectomy surgical bed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rebound extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver and marrow

explanation.summary: Post-splenectomy leukocytosis and thrombocytosis occur because cells the spleen used to store stay in the blood.
