explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients with asplenia show persistent leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, especially in the first weeks to months after splenectomy. Platelets and white blood cells that are normally stored in the spleen instead remain in the circulation, elevating blood counts, and these increased counts raise the risk of thrombosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A myeloproliferative disorder is a primary marrow neoplasm and is not the expected explanation for counts that rise predictably after splenectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An unrecognized infection would be expected to cause fever and local wound findings, which this asymptomatic patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Occult bleeding would lower the hemoglobin and produce symptoms; it does not explain a simultaneous leukocytosis in a well patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs when the bone marrow cannot synthesize blood cells, which is not the situation after removal of a normal spleen.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient who underwent splenectomy several years ago shows abnormal red blood cells with a central bullseye appearance. These cells are best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Target cells are abnormal red blood cells with a bullseye appearance seen in asplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells can be seen on the smear in patients with reduced or absent splenic function. These are abnormal red blood cells with a bullseye appearance, and they also occur in thalassemia, liver disease, and hemoglobinopathies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Howell-Jolly bodies are small dark nuclear DNA remnants inside red blood cells, not a bullseye pattern of the whole cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Schistocytes are fragmented red blood cells and do not show the bullseye appearance described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickled cells are elongated, crescent-shaped red cells seen in sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spherocytes are round cells lacking central pallor and are characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with congenital asplenia has completed vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, and meningococcus. His hematologist plans to start daily antibiotic prophylaxis because of his age. Which of the following is usually the antibiotic of choice?

explanation.summary: Penicillin is usually the antibiotic of choice for prophylaxis in asplenia and hyposplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients with asplenia or hyposplenia receive antibiotic prophylaxis to reduce the risk of infection, since these infections can be lethal. Penicillin is usually the antibiotic of choice, and its use is determined on an individual basis, most often in patients who are young, immunocompromised, or have a history of sepsis from encapsulated bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is not the agent identified for routine prophylaxis in patients without a spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciprofloxacin is not the recommended prophylactic agent for asplenia in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and protozoa and does not cover the encapsulated organisms that threaten asplenic patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin is a parenteral agent used for treatment of resistant gram-positive infections, not daily oral prophylaxis in asplenia.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who underwent splenectomy 4 years ago after a motor vehicle accident calls about 6 hours of fever and chills. In clinic her temperature is 38.9 C (102.0 F), her other vital signs are normal, she appears well, and her examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer a pneumococcal vaccine booster today

choices.label: C
choices.text: Draw blood cultures and schedule follow-up in 24 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obtain CT of the abdomen before any treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prescribe acetaminophen and advise observation at home

explanation.summary: Fever in an asplenic patient demands immediate empiric antibiotics because of the risk of overwhelming sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with asplenia have a high chance of blood-borne infections from encapsulated organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae type B, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Neisseria meningitidis, because the antibodies normally produced by splenic B cells for opsonization are absent. These can be life-threatening infections with overwhelming sepsis, so any asplenic patient with fever requires immediate empiric antibiotic treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vaccination is preventive and is given before infection occurs; it does not treat an acute febrile illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cultures are useful, but deferring treatment for a day in an asplenic patient with fever risks overwhelming sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imaging may follow, but antibiotics must not be delayed for a scan in an asplenic patient with fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symptomatic treatment at home leaves a potentially fulminant encapsulated organism infection untreated.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is evaluated after blunt trauma to the left upper quadrant. CT of the abdomen with contrast shows a splenic laceration with an intrasplenic hematoma and peritoneal blood. Which of the following complete blood count patterns is most likely?

explanation.summary: Splenic rupture typically produces a falling hemoglobin together with thrombocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A complete blood count in splenic rupture may reveal a drop in hemoglobin from blood loss. It also shows thrombocytosis, because platelets enter the circulation during the hemorrhage and these released platelets can no longer be stored in the damaged spleen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombocytopenia is characteristic of platelet sequestration in a congested, enlarged spleen, not of an acutely ruptured one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin falls rather than rises when blood is lost into the peritoneum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute blood loss lowers the hemoglobin, and leukopenia is not the expected consequence of splenic hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancytopenia reflects hypersplenism from a chronically overactive spleen, which is the opposite of this acute picture.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is struck in the left flank during a fall. Her heart rate is 78/min and her blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft without guarding or peritoneal signs. CT with contrast shows a small splenic laceration without active contrast extravasation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Close monitoring with serial abdominal examinations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy of the abdomen within 24 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emergent exploratory laparotomy with splenic repair

choices.label: E
choices.text: Percutaneous catheter drainage of the spleen

explanation.summary: A hemodynamically stable patient without peritoneal signs may be observed with serial abdominal exams.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of splenic rupture depends on the severity and etiology of the injury. Hemodynamically stable patients without peritoneal signs may be observed with close monitoring and serial abdominal examinations rather than taken to the operating room.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Diagnostic laparoscopy is used urgently in unstable patients with evidence of bleeding, not electively in a stable one already imaged by CT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urgent laparotomy is indicated for hemodynamic instability or peritoneal signs, neither of which is present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy is performed when a ruptured spleen cannot be repaired, not for a small laceration in a stable patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Percutaneous drainage is a treatment option for splenic abscess, not for traumatic laceration.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a splenic laceration from blunt trauma has a heart rate of 96/min and a blood pressure of 118/72 mm Hg after fluid resuscitation. Over 12 hours her hemoglobin drifts down and repeat imaging shows ongoing slow bleeding from the spleen without free-flowing hemorrhage. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy for 7 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endovascular embolization of the splenic artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observation alone with serial abdominal examinations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Percutaneous catheter drainage of an intrasplenic collection

explanation.summary: Endovascular embolization is used in the more stable patient who has slow ongoing splenic bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of splenic rupture depends on severity. Endovascular embolization can be used in patients who are more stable but who have slow bleeding, occupying the space between pure observation and urgent operation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics treat splenic abscess and asplenic sepsis; they do nothing to stop bleeding from a lacerated spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exploratory laparotomy is reserved for severe blood loss or hemodynamic instability, and this patient has been stabilized.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Observation alone is appropriate for stable patients without peritoneal signs, but her hemoglobin is falling from demonstrated ongoing bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Percutaneous drainage addresses an intrasplenic pus collection in splenic abscess, not active hemorrhage.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man being treated for infective endocarditis develops persistent fever and left upper quadrant pain. CT of the abdomen demonstrates an intrasplenic fluid collection, and diagnostic needle aspiration is performed for culture. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be recovered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anaerobic gut flora such as Bacteroides species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fungal organisms such as Candida species

explanation.summary: Splenic abscesses complicating endocarditis are most often caused by staph, strep, and enterococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic abscesses typically occur due to systemic bacteremia, often as a complication of infective endocarditis. The most common organisms responsible are staph, strep, and enterococcus after endocarditis, with gastrointestinal or respiratory pathogens implicated when the bacterial source lies in those areas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrointestinal pathogens are implicated when the bacterial source is the gut, not in an abscess seeded from endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fungi are seen in immunocompromised patients, who are at higher risk, rather than in a typical post-endocarditis abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tuberculosis is listed among infections that cause splenomegaly through increased splenic immune activity, not as a common abscess isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neisseria meningitidis is an encapsulated organism that threatens asplenic patients; it is not the usual cause of an abscess after endocarditis.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a splenic abscess has received intravenous fluids and appropriate intravenous antibiotics, and percutaneous drainage was performed. After 10 days he remains febrile, and repeat CT shows a persistent intrasplenic collection. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat needle aspiration for culture only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transition to oral antibiotics and discharge home

explanation.summary: Splenectomy is required when a splenic abscess fails to resolve with antibiotics and drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of splenic abscess is with intravenous fluids and appropriate antibiotics, and percutaneous drainage is performed in select cases. Some patients require splenectomy if the infection fails to resolve, which is the situation here after 10 days of persistent fever and a residual collection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Embolization is a treatment for slow bleeding after splenic rupture, and it is itself a cause of iatrogenic splenic abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serial examination is the approach for a stable traumatic splenic injury, not for a persistently infected spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeat aspiration for culture alone gathers information without addressing an abscess that has not responded to source control.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stepping down to oral therapy abandons an infection that has already failed intravenous antibiotics and drainage.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is admitted with fever, left upper quadrant pain, and leukocytosis, and CT of the abdomen shows a splenic abscess. Which of the following elements of her history is a recognized risk factor for this condition?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia treated with oral iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migraine with aura treated with sumatriptan

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seasonal asthma controlled with an inhaler

explanation.summary: Thrombotic states such as antiphospholipid syndrome predispose to splenic abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: Risk factors for splenic abscess include endocarditis, splenomegaly, atrial fibrillation, which causes thromboemboli, and thrombotic states such as antiphospholipid syndrome. Her recurrent thrombosis places her in that last category.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Treated hypothyroidism is not among the conditions that predispose to splenic abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency anemia is not among the listed risk factors for an intrasplenic pus collection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Migraine with aura has no established relationship to splenic abscess formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asthma is not a recognized predisposing condition for splenic abscess.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A cyanotic newborn is found to have complex cardiac malformations. Abdominal imaging demonstrates an abnormal arrangement of the intra-abdominal organs, and no splenic tissue can be identified. Which of the following best describes this infant's splenic disorder?

explanation.summary: Congenital asplenia accompanies abnormal abdominal organ arrangement and congenital heart disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital asplenia is usually associated with an abnormal arrangement of the intra-abdominal organs and with congenital heart disease. These patients often present with associated intraabdominal disorders and congenital heart disease, and they may also present with sepsis due to infection from encapsulated organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An accessory spleen is extra healthy splenic tissue separate from the main spleen, so splenic tissue would be identified rather than absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypersplenism is an overactive spleen that removes blood cells too quickly, which requires a spleen to be present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Physiologic asplenia describes a present but nonfunctioning spleen, classically after auto-infarction in sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic rupture follows trauma to an existing spleen and is not a congenital finding in a newborn.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: Hyposplenia, defined as a spleen with decreased splenic function, is most commonly the result of which of the following conditions?

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease is the most common cause of hyposplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyposplenia is a spleen with decreased splenic function and is more common than complete asplenia. Its most common cause is sickle cell disease, in which repeated vaso-occlusive crises within the spleen progressively damage the organ and reduce its function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic alcohol use leads to cirrhosis and congestive splenomegaly rather than being the leading cause of reduced splenic function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is a coagulation factor deficiency and does not impair splenic function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency anemia does not feature rigid cells that damage the spleen and is not a listed cause of hyposplenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without producing a hypofunctional spleen.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has massive splenomegaly of unknown cause. Bone marrow and lymph node biopsies are nondiagnostic, and liver biopsy is unrevealing. The surgical team recommends diagnostic splenectomy rather than percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen. Which of the following best supports this choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Needle biopsy cannot obtain tissue adequate for any culture

choices.label: B
choices.text: Needle biopsy is contraindicated after a lymph node biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Needle biopsy of the spleen requires general anesthesia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenectomy cures most underlying causes of splenomegaly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic pathology may be patchy and missed on an isolated biopsy

explanation.summary: Splenectomy is often preferred to needle biopsy because splenic pathology can be patchy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of bleeding risks, splenic biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis remains unknown after other biopsies and studies, as is the case here. In many such cases splenectomy is preferred to needle biopsy, since the splenic pathology may be patchy and therefore not seen on an isolated biopsy sample.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Needle aspiration can yield material for culture, as it does when guided aspiration of a splenic abscess is performed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A prior lymph node biopsy does not contraindicate splenic sampling; bone marrow and lymph node biopsies are the studies performed before considering splenic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stated concern about needle biopsy is sampling error and bleeding risk, not an anesthetic requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy here is diagnostic; treatment of splenomegaly is aimed at the underlying cause, which removal of the spleen does not cure.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is found to have splenomegaly on abdominal imaging. She also reports several months of joint pain, a facial rash over her cheeks and nose, and intermittent pleuritic chest pain. Which of the following laboratory tests best targets the suspected underlying cause of her splenomegaly?

explanation.summary: Additional laboratory workup for splenomegaly is directed at the suspected underlying disease, and antinuclear antibody is used for suspected lupus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lab results can indicate the underlying cause of splenomegaly, and depending on the presentation additional laboratory workup may be necessary. Antinuclear antibody testing is used for suspected systemic lupus erythematosus, and lupus is one of the autoimmune disorders that enlarges the spleen through increased splenic immune activity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease and the thalassemias, which this presentation does not suggest.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rheumatoid factor is the test used when rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, and her rash and pleuritic pain point to lupus instead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum amylase evaluates pancreatic inflammation, which is relevant to local spread causing splenic abscess rather than to this picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum ferritin assesses iron stores and does not evaluate an autoimmune cause of splenomegaly.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with a body mass index of 41 kg/m2 undergoes abdominal ultrasound for suspected gallstones. The study incidentally shows an enlarged spleen, although no spleen was palpable during a careful abdominal examination performed earlier that day. Which of the following best explains this discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An enlarged spleen becomes palpable only after it infarcts

choices.label: B
choices.text: An enlarged spleen may not be palpable when masked by obesity

choices.label: C
choices.text: The spleen becomes palpable only after it doubles in size

choices.label: D
choices.text: The spleen can be palpated only in the right lateral decubitus position

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultrasound systematically overestimates splenic size in obesity

explanation.summary: Not all enlarged spleens are palpable, and obesity can mask splenomegaly on examination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenomegaly is often asymptomatic and is most often found on physical exam as a left upper quadrant mass that becomes more prominent below the left ribcage with deep inspiration. However, not all enlarged spleens are palpable, and an enlarged spleen may not be palpable if it is masked by obesity, so imaging can reveal splenomegaly that examination missed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infarction shrinks the spleen to a fibrous remnant and has nothing to do with whether an enlarged spleen can be felt.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A spleen is usually palpable after approximately 40% enlargement rather than requiring a doubling in size.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen is palpated in both the supine and right lateral decubitus positions, not exclusively in one of them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abdominal ultrasound is the best test for measuring the size of the spleen, so its measurement is the more reliable of the two findings.

questions.topicName: Disorders of the Spleen

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is examining an H&E-stained section of a child's thymus at low power. In the paler central region of a lobe, she notes a distinctive spherical structure composed of keratinized epithelial reticular cells arranged in concentric layers. Within which of the following regions of the thymus is this structure located?

explanation.summary: Thymic (Hassall) corpuscles are found in the medulla of the thymus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The structure described is a thymic corpuscle (Hassall corpuscle), a collection of keratinized epithelial reticular cells layered concentrically. These corpuscles are located within the medulla, the paler central region of each thymic lobe.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The corticomedullary junction is the border where mature T cells exit through postcapillary venules, not the site of thymic corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The capsule is a thin fibrous outer covering and does not contain thymic corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interlobular septa are fibrous extensions of the capsule that divide the cortex into lobules and contain no thymic corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The cortex is the densely packed outer region; thymic corpuscles are a medullary feature.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A physiology instructor asks a student to summarize the single main function of the thymus in the immune system. Which of the following best describes this function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Differentiation of B cells into plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regulation of the basal metabolic rate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removal of aged and damaged erythrocytes

explanation.summary: The thymus's one main function is the production of mature T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus serves as a training ground where T-cell precursors from the bone marrow undergo positive and negative selection to become mature T cells capable of participating in the adaptive immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-cell differentiation occurs in the bone marrow and lymphoid tissues, not the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells derived from B cells; mature T cells can potentiate this but the thymus itself does not produce antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Regulation of the basal metabolic rate is a function of the thyroid gland, not the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Removal of aged and damaged erythrocytes is a function of the spleen.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of drooping eyelids and generalized weakness that worsens toward the end of the day. Testing confirms myasthenia gravis, and a chest x-ray reveals an anterior mediastinal mass. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the mass?

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis with an anterior mediastinal mass is classically associated with a thymoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: About half of patients with a thymoma also have myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease with antibodies against the neuromuscular junction. Because this form of myasthenia is potentially curable, a chest CT is done in all newly diagnosed patients to look for a thymoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphomas (such as T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma) can occur in the thymus but are not linked to myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Teratomas can present as thymic masses but are not associated with myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymic carcinoma is a rapidly growing thymic malignancy and is not the classic association with myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymic hyperplasia reflects rapid growth of thymic cells and is not the classic cause of a mass in a patient with myasthenia gravis.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A newborn is noted to have a cleft palate, a holosystolic murmur, and poor muscle tone. A chest x-ray shows an absent thymic shadow, and serum calcium is low. Which of the following best explains the underlying developmental defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chromosome 22 deletion causing abnormal development

choices.label: B
choices.text: Age-related loss of thymic cells at roughly 3% per year

choices.label: C
choices.text: An X-linked recessive mutation in the WAS gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of positive selection of T cells in the thymic cortex

explanation.summary: DiGeorge syndrome results from a chromosome 22 deletion that disrupts neural crest-derived development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
explanation.whyCorrect: DiGeorge syndrome is a congenital disorder caused by a gene deletion on chromosome 22 that leads to failure of normal neural crest development, producing abnormal third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. This causes thymic hypoplasia (absent thymic shadow), parathyroid hypoplasia (hypocalcemia), and congenital heart disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Age-related thymic hypoplasia occurs gradually in adulthood and does not explain a congenital defect in a newborn.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A WAS gene mutation causes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, characterized by eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections, not this pharyngeal pouch phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoantibodies against the neuromuscular junction cause myasthenia gravis, which is associated with thymoma rather than congenital thymic hypoplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure of positive selection describes a step in normal T-cell development, not the congenital cause of an absent thymus with hypocalcemia.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A pathology resident compares the cortex and medulla of a thymus on an H&E-stained slide. The medulla appears distinctly paler than the darkly basophilic cortex. Which of the following best explains why the medulla stains more lightly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains fewer densely packed lymphocytes and more epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is composed mostly of fatty tissue that has replaced lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is surrounded by a thick fibrous capsule that blocks staining

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks any epithelial reticular cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its lymphocytes are more tightly packed than those of the cortex

explanation.summary: The medulla is paler because it has fewer densely packed lymphocytes and more epithelial cells, whose cytoplasm is eosinophilic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cortex appears dark blue (basophilic) because lymphocytes are packed closely together. The medulla contains fewer densely packed lymphocytes and more epithelial cells, which have more eosinophilic cytoplasm, giving it a paler appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty replacement occurs gradually with age throughout the whole thymus and is not the reason the medulla is paler than the cortex on a childhood section.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fibrous capsule surrounds the whole organ and does not selectively lighten medullary staining.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The medulla is actually rich in epithelial cells, including those forming thymic corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lymphocytes are more tightly packed in the cortex, which is why the cortex, not the medulla, stains darkly.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: An immunology student is studying the blood-thymus barrier, which makes it nearly impossible for circulating antigens in the blood to enter the thymus. Which of the following best explains why maintaining this barrier is important?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating antigens would cause the thymus to fuse with the thyroid gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating antigens would disrupt the normal process of T-cell selection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating antigens would prevent B cells from entering the medulla

choices.label: D
choices.text: Circulating antigens would stimulate excessive antibody production by thymocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Circulating antigens would trigger fatty replacement of the thymus

explanation.summary: The blood-thymus barrier keeps blood-borne antigens out so they cannot disrupt T-cell selection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The barrier is formed by epithelial-reticular cells joined by tight junctions and nonfenestrated thymic cortical capillaries. It prevents circulating antigens from entering the thymus, because exposure to such antigens would disrupt the normal positive and negative selection of developing T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no mechanism by which antigens cause the thymus to fuse with the thyroid; severe hyperplasia may merely be mistaken for an enlarged thyroid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The barrier's purpose is to protect T-cell selection, not to control B-cell entry into the medulla.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymocytes are developing T cells and do not produce antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fatty replacement of the thymus is an age-related process, not a consequence of antigen exposure across the barrier.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: During T-cell development, a developing T cell in the thymic medulla is presented with a self-antigen by an antigen-presenting cell and binds to it very strongly. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It differentiates into a regulatory T (Treg) cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: It enters the peripheral circulation as a helper T cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is destroyed by apoptosis because it is autoreactive

choices.label: D
choices.text: It matures into a B cell that secretes antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: It migrates back to the cortex for positive selection

explanation.summary: During negative selection in the medulla, T cells that bind self-antigen too strongly are deemed autoreactive and destroyed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Negative selection occurs in the medulla, where T cells are again presented with self-antigens by antigen-presenting cells. If a T cell binds too strongly, it is deemed autoreactive and destroyed by apoptosis, preventing reactions against the body's own tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intermediate binding to self-antigen leads a cell to become a regulatory T (Treg) cell, not strong binding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Weak binding to self-antigen leads to positive selection and entry into the peripheral circulation, not strong binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T cells never become B cells; the two are separate lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Positive selection occurs earlier in the cortex; cells do not migrate back to the cortex after reaching the medulla.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A developing T cell has just arrived in the thymic cortex from the bone marrow. It is presented with self-antigens but fails to recognize them. Which of the following is the most likely outcome for this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes a cytotoxic CD8+ T cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: It immediately exits into the systemic circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is stored in a thymic corpuscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: It progresses inward to the medulla for negative selection

explanation.summary: During positive selection in the cortex, T cells that fail to recognize self-antigens undergo apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In positive selection, developing T cells in the cortex are presented with self-antigens. Those that recognize and react to self-antigens progress inward to the medulla, while those that fail to recognize self-antigens undergo apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Differentiation into CD4+ or CD8+ cells occurs after successful completion of selection, not after failing positive selection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cells exit into the systemic circulation only after completing both positive and negative selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymic corpuscles are concentric collections of keratinized epithelial cells and do not store T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only cells that successfully recognize self-antigens progress to the medulla; a cell that fails positive selection does not advance.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A radiologist notes that the thymus is easily seen as a sharply demarcated, sail-shaped structure on the chest x-ray of a healthy neonate, yet it is not visible on the chest x-ray of a healthy 40-year-old. Which of the following best explains why the thymus becomes less visible in the adult?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The adult thymus becomes densely calcified and radiolucent

choices.label: B
choices.text: The adult thymus is shielded by the developing sternum only after puberty

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thymus involutes and loses cells while the chest enlarges with growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thymus is replaced by a rapidly growing thymic carcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: The thymus migrates out of the mediastinum into the neck

explanation.summary: The thymus is most visible in the neonate and becomes harder to see in adults as it involutes while the chest grows.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus is most easily seen on a neonate's chest x-ray because thymic size is at its maximum while the chest is small. As a child grows, the thymus involutes (losing roughly 3% of its cells per year) and the chest enlarges, making the thymus less visible in adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adult thymus becomes fatty and shrinks rather than becoming densely calcified.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sternum lies in front of the thymus at all ages and is not what makes the adult thymus invisible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of visibility is a normal aging process, not the result of a thymic carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus stays in the superior mediastinum; it does not migrate into the neck with age.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a large anterior mediastinal mass develops swelling of the face and neck, distended veins across his chest, and shortness of breath. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletion of a gene on the long arm of chromosome 22

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of thymic negative selection producing autoreactive T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of blood flow through the superior vena cava by the mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced cell-based immunity caused by age-related thymic involution

explanation.summary: Mediastinal neoplasms can compress the superior vena cava, producing superior vena cava syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mediastinal neoplasms such as thymoma and lymphoma can be associated with superior vena cava syndrome, a constellation of signs that occur when blood flow through the superior vena cava is blocked by the mass. This causes face and neck swelling, upper extremity swelling, dyspnea, cough, and dilated collateral chest veins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoantibodies at the neuromuscular junction cause the muscle weakness of myasthenia gravis, not facial swelling and distended chest veins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A chromosome 22 deletion causes congenital DiGeorge syndrome, not superior vena cava obstruction in an adult.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of negative selection leads to autoimmune disease, not the venous congestion described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Age-related thymic involution reduces immune function but does not cause superior vena cava obstruction.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy has a history of recurrent ear and sinus infections, widespread eczema, and easy bruising. Laboratory studies show thrombocytopenia with unusually small platelets. This X-linked recessive condition is caused by a mutation in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gene controlling positive selection in the cortex

choices.label: B
choices.text: A gene encoding a neuromuscular junction receptor

explanation.summary: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by WAS gene mutations, producing recurrent infections, eczema, and thrombocytopenia with small platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome results from abnormalities of the WAS gene and produces a triad of recurrent infections (from a hypoplastic/aplastic thymus), eczema, and thrombocytopenia with small platelets, matching this patient's presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Positive selection is a normal step of T-cell development and is not the gene defect underlying this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A neuromuscular junction defect underlies myasthenia gravis, which causes muscle weakness, not this triad.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chromosome 22 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome, which features parathyroid hypoplasia and congenital heart disease rather than eczema and small-platelet thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-globin gene defects cause alpha-thalassemia, a red cell disorder unrelated to this immunodeficiency triad.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man has had several respiratory infections over the past year and mounts a weak antibody response to the influenza vaccine. His physician attributes this in part to reduced cell-based immunity. Which of the following age-related changes in the thymus best accounts for this decline?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rapidly growing thymic carcinoma replacing normal tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blockade of the neuromuscular junction by autoantibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the blood-thymus barrier allowing antigens to enter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gradual loss of thymic cells at roughly 3% per year

explanation.summary: Age-related thymic hypoplasia results from the normal ongoing loss of thymic cells, decreasing cell-based immunity in older adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: Age-related thymic hypoplasia is a consequence of the normal loss of thymic cells throughout adulthood (about 3% per year). This reduced thymic function decreases cell-based immunity, contributing to more infections and malignancies and to decreased responsiveness to vaccines in older patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chromosome 22 deletion causes congenital DiGeorge syndrome, not a gradual decline appearing in an 82-year-old.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A thymic carcinoma is a malignancy that presents as a mass, not the normal age-related decline described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoantibody blockade of the neuromuscular junction causes myasthenia gravis, not reduced vaccine responsiveness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure of the blood-thymus barrier would disrupt T-cell selection but is not the described mechanism of age-related immune decline.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A researcher traces a developing T cell backward in time, from the moment it arrives in the thymic cortex to the site where its precursor was originally formed. In which of the following sites was this precursor formed?

explanation.summary: T cell precursors are formed in the bone marrow and then migrate to the thymus.
explanation.whyCorrect: T cell precursors are formed in the bone marrow, from which they migrate to the thymus. Only after reaching the thymic cortex do they begin positive selection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymph nodes participate in B cell differentiation; T cell precursors arise in the bone marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spleen removes aged and damaged erythrocytes and is not the site of T cell precursor formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymic cortex is where the precursor arrives and undergoes positive selection, not where it is formed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymic medulla is the site of negative selection, which occurs after the cell has already formed and been positively selected.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: An embryology instructor asks a student to identify the structures from which the thymus is derived. Which of the following is the correct embryologic origin of the thymus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ventral endodermal outgrowth of the dorsal mesentery

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first and second pairs of pharyngeal pouches and clefts

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fourth and sixth pairs of pharyngeal arches and their cartilages

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second and third pairs of pharyngeal arches and their muscles

choices.label: E
choices.text: The third and, inconstantly, the fourth pairs of pharyngeal pouches

explanation.summary: The thymus is derived embryologically from the third and, inconstantly, the fourth pair of pharyngeal pouches.
explanation.whyCorrect: Embryologically, the thymus arises from the third and, inconstantly, the fourth pair of pharyngeal pouches. This shared origin is why disordered pharyngeal pouch development affects the thymus and the parathyroid glands together.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The thymus is not derived from the dorsal mesentery; it is a pharyngeal pouch derivative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first and second pouches are not the source of thymic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fourth and sixth arches give rise to other structures and are not the origin of the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus arises from pharyngeal pouches, which are endodermal outpocketings, not from the pharyngeal arches.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: At autopsy, the thymus of a 55-year-old man is small, soft, and distinctly yellow, unlike the grayish-pink lumpy organ seen in a child. Which of the following best accounts for this change in appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of keratin within the medullary thymic corpuscles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of hemosiderin from repeated intrathymic hemorrhage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expansion of the darkly basophilic cortex of each lobule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrous thickening of the interlobular connective tissue septa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infiltration and replacement of thymic tissue by fatty tissue

explanation.summary: Around puberty, fatty tissue begins to infiltrate and replace thymic tissue, making the thymus smaller and more yellow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus is grayish-pink and lumpy during childhood. Around the time of puberty, fatty tissue begins to infiltrate and replace the thymic tissue, and throughout the rest of life the thymus slowly shrinks and becomes more yellow in appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Keratinized epithelial reticular cells form thymic corpuscles in the medulla, but these do not turn the whole organ yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin deposition is not described as a feature of the aging thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The basophilic cortex shrinks rather than expands as the thymus involutes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interlobular septa are thin extensions of the capsule that divide the cortex into lobules; their thickening is not the cause of the yellow color.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: On low-power microscopy of a child's thymus, the outer region of each lobe is subdivided into irregularly shaped lobules by thin partitions of connective tissue. These partitions are extensions of which of the following?

explanation.summary: Interlobular septa are thin extensions of the thymic fibrous capsule that divide the cortex into lobules.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus is surrounded by a thin, fibrous tissue capsule. The cortex is separated into irregularly shaped lobules by thin extensions of that fibrous capsule, called interlobular septa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The corticomedullary junction is the border where mature T cells exit through postcapillary venules, not a source of septa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pericardium surrounds the heart and does not contribute the septa dividing the thymic cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The medullary epithelial network contains thymic corpuscles but does not form the connective tissue septa of the cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The visceral pleura covers the lungs and does not send septa into the thymus.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A student views a high-power field of thymic cortex. The overwhelmingly predominant cell is small, with a darkly staining central nucleus and very little surrounding cytoplasm. Which of the following is this cell?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keratinized cell of a thymic corpuscle

explanation.summary: The thymus is composed mostly of small T cells (thymocytes), which have a darkly staining central nucleus and scant cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus is composed mostly of small T cells, also known as T lymphocytes or thymocytes. These are lymphocytes with a darkly staining central nucleus and very little surrounding cytoplasm, and their dense packing gives the cortex its basophilic appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dendritic cells serve as antigen-presenting cells during negative selection in the medulla and are not the predominant cortical cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epithelial reticular cells have more abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and are concentrated in the medulla.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Keratinized epithelial reticular cells form the concentric thymic corpuscles found in the medulla, not the small dark cortical cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and are not the cell that fills the thymic cortex.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: An investigator studying why blood-borne antigens cannot reach developing T cells examines the capillaries of the thymic cortex by electron microscopy. Which of the following features of these capillaries helps maintain the barrier?

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are lined by keratinized epithelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: They drain directly into thymic corpuscles

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack a surrounding basement membrane

explanation.summary: Thymic cortical capillaries have a nonfenestrated endothelium, which is one of the two components of the blood-thymus barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The blood-thymus barrier has two parts: epithelial-reticular cells joined by tight junctions, and thymic cortical capillaries with a nonfenestrated endothelium. Because these capillaries lack fenestrae, they are far less permeable to circulating antigens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fenestrae are holes that would make the capillary more permeable to antigens, which is exactly what the barrier prevents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Keratinized epithelial reticular cells form thymic corpuscles in the medulla; they do not line capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymic corpuscles are solid concentric collections of keratinized cells and are not a vascular drainage site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of a basement membrane is not a described feature of thymic cortical capillaries and would not tighten the barrier.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: The epithelial-reticular cells of the thymus form a net-like scaffolding and are joined to one another by tight junctions. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of these junctions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They allow antigens free access to the developing thymocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: They block epithelial-reticular cells from presenting antigen to thymocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: They convert epithelial-reticular cells into phagocytic macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: They create fenestrations that increase capillary permeability

choices.label: E
choices.text: They prevent molecules and cell products from passing between adjacent cells

explanation.summary: Tight junctions between epithelial-reticular cells prevent molecules such as antigens and cell products from passing between adjacent cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epithelial-reticular cells (ERCs) provide a net-like scaffolding for the thymus, and the tight junctions connecting them prevent the passage of molecules (eg, antigens) and cell products in between two adjacent ERCs. This is half of the blood-thymus barrier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The purpose of the barrier is the opposite: circulating antigens are kept away from developing T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ERCs are themselves one of the antigen-presenting cell types important in thymic T cell maturation, so their junctions do not block antigen presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epithelial-reticular cells are not converted into macrophages by their junctions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fenestrations are a property of certain capillary endothelia, not something created by epithelial tight junctions.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A developing T cell in the thymus engages a self-antigen presented on MHC II with intermediate binding strength. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes an epithelial-reticular cell of the medulla

choices.label: B
choices.text: It fails positive selection and dies within the cortex

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is deemed autoreactive and destroyed by apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is positively selected and becomes a regulatory T cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: It remains permanently in the medulla as a dendritic cell

explanation.summary: Intermediate binding to self-antigen results in positive selection and differentiation into a regulatory T (Treg) cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Binding strength to self-antigen determines fate: strong binding leads to negative selection and apoptosis, weak binding leads to positive selection and release into the peripheral circulation, and intermediate binding leads to positive selection as a regulatory T cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T cells never become epithelial-reticular cells; the two are distinct lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Death in the cortex follows failure to recognize self-antigen at all during positive selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction as an autoreactive cell follows strong, not intermediate, binding to self-antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells of a separate lineage, not a fate of a selected thymocyte.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A T cell has completed both positive and negative selection and is ready to join the systemic blood stream. Through which of the following does it leave the thymus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Efferent lymphatics draining the thymic capsule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fenestrated capillaries within the outer cortex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic sinuses surrounding the thymic corpuscles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postcapillary venules at the corticomedullary junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thoracic duct tributaries within the interlobular septa

explanation.summary: Mature T cells exit the thymus via postcapillary venules at the corticomedullary junction.
explanation.whyCorrect: After successive completion of positive and negative selection, T cells differentiate into CD4+ or CD8+ cells and exit the thymus via postcapillary venules located at the corticomedullary junction, entering the systemic blood stream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Exit is venous rather than through efferent lymphatics of the capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thymic cortical capillaries are nonfenestrated and form part of the blood-thymus barrier rather than an exit route.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymic corpuscles are solid concentric collections of keratinized epithelial reticular cells with no lymphatic sinuses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The interlobular septa are connective tissue extensions of the capsule and are not the described exit pathway.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A student is asked what thymocytes become after they have successfully completed both positive and negative selection. Which of the following pairs correctly names these more specialized cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4+ helper cells and CD8+ cytotoxic cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4+ regulatory cells and plasma cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD8+ helper cells and memory B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural killer cells and dendritic cells

explanation.summary: Selected thymocytes differentiate into CD4+ helper T cells or CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: After successive completion of positive and negative selection, the T cells differentiate into more specialized cells, including CD4+ cells (helper T cells) and CD8+ cells (cytotoxic T cells), which then exit into the systemic circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma cells are of B cell lineage and are not a product of thymic selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The labels are reversed: CD4+ marks helper cells and CD8+ marks cytotoxic cells, and B cells are not thymic products.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epithelial-reticular cells form the thymic scaffolding and are not derived from thymocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dendritic cells act as antigen-presenting cells during negative selection rather than arising from selected thymocytes.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: In an experimental model, medullary antigen-presenting cells are engineered so that they can no longer eliminate thymocytes that bind self-antigen strongly. These animals are at greatest risk of developing which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune disease such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recurrent bacterial and fungal infections from T cell deficiency

explanation.summary: Failure of negative selection leaves autoreactive T cells alive, which can lead to autoimmune disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Negative selection in the medulla destroys T cells that bind self-antigen too strongly, since such cells would react against the body's own tissues. Failure to properly destroy autoreactive T cells during negative selection can lead to autoimmune diseases like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A slow-growing anterior mediastinal malignancy describes a thymoma, which is not a consequence of defective negative selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parathyroid hypoplasia with hypocalcemia is a feature of DiGeorge syndrome from abnormal pharyngeal pouch development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrent infection results from too few functional T cells, as in thymic hypoplasia, not from surviving autoreactive clones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small-platelet thrombocytopenia is part of the Wiskott-Aldrich triad caused by WAS gene abnormalities.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: An immunologist describes the thymus as a competitive training ground in which only a small minority of developing T cells pass its rigorous testing. Which of the following best describes what those surviving cells do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are incorporated into the thymic corpuscles of the medulla

choices.label: B
choices.text: They differentiate into plasma cells that secrete circulating antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: They leave the thymus and patrol the body for pathogens and cancer cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: They remain in the thymic medulla as antigen-presenting cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: They return to the bone marrow to generate new lymphoid precursors

explanation.summary: The few T cells that pass thymic selection leave the thymus and participate in the body's immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vast majority of T cells fail to meet the thymus' high standards and undergo apoptosis. The few T cells that pass muster leave the thymus and participate in the body's immune response, patrolling it for invading pathogens and cancer cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thymic corpuscles are concentric collections of keratinized epithelial reticular cells and do not house T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma cells arise from B cells; T cells can potentiate antibody secretion but do not become plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antigen presentation in the medulla is performed by epithelial-reticular cells, B cells, and dendritic cells, not by the graduating T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Precursor formation happens in the bone marrow before thymic entry; selected T cells do not return there.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A clinician is counseling a trainee about who typically presents with a thymoma. Which of the following statements best describes the usual demographics of these patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most are adolescents in the second decade of life

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most are adults older than 40 years of age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most are children younger than 10 years of age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nearly all are men younger than 30 years of age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly all are women of childbearing age

explanation.summary: Thymomas usually occur in adults older than 40 and affect males and females equally.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thymomas usually occur in adults older than 40 years of age and are rare in children. Males and females are affected equally.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adolescence is not the peak age; thymomas favor adults older than 40.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymomas are specifically described as rare in children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no male predominance, and young adulthood is not the typical age of presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no female predominance; males and females are affected equally.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with myasthenia gravis after developing ptosis and fatigable generalized weakness. She has no respiratory symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?

explanation.summary: Every newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis patient gets a chest CT to look for a thymoma, because thymoma-associated myasthenia is potentially curable.
explanation.whyCorrect: Half of patients with thymomas also have myasthenia gravis. Because this is a potentially curable form of myasthenia, a CT scan of the chest is done in all newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis patients to identify a thymic mass and define its extent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thyroid biopsy is used when a mediastinal mass must be distinguished from a massively enlarged thyroid, not as the initial step in myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow sampling is not part of the evaluation of newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypocalcemia relates to parathyroid hypoplasia in DiGeorge syndrome, not to myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A chromosome 22 deletion causes congenital DiGeorge syndrome and would not explain adult-onset myasthenia gravis.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has an anterior mediastinal mass that has enlarged markedly over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows a malignant neoplasm of thymic epithelial origin. Which of the following terms best describes a rapidly growing malignancy of the thymus?

explanation.summary: Rapidly growing thymic malignancies are termed thymic carcinoma, in contrast to slow-growing thymomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: An enlarged thymic mass may be due to simple hyperplasia or to thymic malignancy. Slow-growing thymic malignancies are termed thymomas, whereas rapidly growing malignancies are termed thymic carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma is a lymphoid rather than thymic epithelial malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Teratomas are another mass that can present within the thymus but are not thymic epithelial carcinomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperplasia is rapid growth of thymic cells but is not a malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymoma denotes the slow-growing thymic malignancy, the opposite of the tempo described here.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has dyspnea and a large anterior mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows sheets of immature lymphoid cells of T-cell lineage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Lymphomas presenting within the thymus are specifically T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Besides thymoma and thymic carcinoma, other malignancies that can present within the thymus are lymphomas, specifically T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, and teratomas. A mass composed of immature T-lineage lymphoid cells fits this entity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperplasia is rapid growth of normal thymic cells rather than a monomorphous immature lymphoid population.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Teratomas are germ cell tumors and would not consist of immature T-lineage lymphoid cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymic carcinoma is a rapidly growing epithelial malignancy, not a sheet of immature lymphoid cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymomas are slow-growing thymic epithelial malignancies and are rare in children.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a large mass occupying the superior mediastinum and extending toward the base of the neck. Imaging cannot determine whether it represents a massively enlarged thyroid gland or severe thymic hyperplasia. Which of the following is most likely required to establish the origin of the mass?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measurement of antibodies against the neuromuscular junction

explanation.summary: Severe thymic hyperplasia can be mistaken for a massively enlarged thyroid, so biopsy is usually needed to determine the origin of the mass.
explanation.whyCorrect: Since severe thymic hyperplasia can easily be mistaken for a massively enlarged thyroid gland, a biopsy is usually required to distinguish the origin of the mass.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping is relevant to congenital disorders such as DiGeorge syndrome, not to distinguishing thymus from thyroid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies against the neuromuscular junction are used in evaluating myasthenia gravis, not in identifying the source of this mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thyroid function testing reflects hormone output and does not establish which organ the mass arose from.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deferring the workup does not answer the question of tissue origin and delays diagnosis.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a chest x-ray for a persistent cough. The radiologist reports a left mediastinal contour abnormality with loss of the silhouette of the upper left heart border, and a lateral film localizes the abnormality to the retrosternal space. This mass lies within which of the following compartments?

explanation.summary: A retrosternal mass causing a mediastinal contour abnormality with loss of the upper left heart border silhouette is an anterior mediastinal mass, typical of a thymic mass.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thymic masses are usually asymptomatic and found on chest x-rays done for other reasons. A thymic mass produces a mediastinal contour abnormality with loss of the silhouette of the upper left heart border, and the lateral radiograph confirms localization to the anterior mediastinum in the retrosternal space. A chest CT then further identifies the extent of the mass.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A pleural process would not be confined to the retrosternal anterior compartment described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Middle mediastinal hilar masses do not produce a retrosternal location on the lateral film.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pericardial location would not appear as a retrosternal anterior mediastinal mass.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A posterior mediastinal mass would not sit in the retrosternal space in front of the heart.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with a large mediastinal mass has facial and upper extremity swelling, dilated collateral chest veins, and now audible stridor with worsening dyspnea. Which of the following most urgently threatens her life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis of circulating autoreactive T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compression of the airway requiring intubation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tetany from a falling serum calcium

explanation.summary: In superior vena cava syndrome the blockage can be severe enough to compress the airway and may require intubation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mediastinal neoplasms such as thymoma and lymphoma can cause superior vena cava syndrome, with face and neck swelling, upper extremity swelling, dyspnea, cough, and dilated collateral chest veins. The blockage can be significant enough to compress the airway and may require intubation, which is the immediate threat signaled by stridor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apoptosis of autoreactive T cells is a normal step of negative selection in the thymus, not a clinical emergency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small-platelet thrombocytopenia is part of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and is unrelated to this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Generalized weakness is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis, which does not explain swelling, collateral veins, or stridor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypocalcemic tetany relates to parathyroid hypoplasia in DiGeorge syndrome, not to a mediastinal mass.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 7-month-old girl with DiGeorge syndrome has a profoundly low T-cell count and has been hospitalized three times for severe pneumonia and sinusitis. Which of the following is most likely to be required for her survival?

explanation.summary: Children with DiGeorge syndrome and very low T-cell counts with severe recurrent infections may require stem cell or thymic transplantation to survive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some children with DiGeorge syndrome develop very low T-cell counts with severe recurrent lung and sinus infections, and they may require stem cell transplantation or thymic transplantation to survive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thyroid hormone replacement addresses thyroid failure, not the T-cell deficiency of thymic aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma exchange removes circulating antibodies and does not correct absent thymic T-cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no thymic mass to resect; the problem is failure of thymic development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing the spleen would further impair immune defense and does not restore T cells.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: Two infants are found to have DiGeorge syndrome. One has an essentially absent thymus, and the other has a small but identifiable thymus. Which of the following best predicts how severe the immunodeficiency will be in each child?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number of thymic corpuscles in the tissue present

choices.label: C
choices.text: The serum calcium concentration at birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: The severity of the cleft palate

choices.label: E
choices.text: The severity of the congenital heart defect

explanation.summary: In DiGeorge syndrome, the degree of immunodeficiency correlates with the degree of thymic hypoplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: DiGeorge syndrome results from a chromosome 22 deletion causing abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, with failure of thymic development, parathyroid hypoplasia, and congenital heart disease. The degree of immunodeficiency in the affected child correlates to the degree of thymic hypoplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Thymic corpuscle counts are not described as a predictor of immune function in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serum calcium reflects parathyroid hypoplasia, which is a separate component of the syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Palatal abnormalities accompany the syndrome but are not what the degree of immunodeficiency tracks with.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congenital heart disease is part of the syndrome but does not predict the severity of immune failure.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome has had repeated bacterial respiratory infections in addition to eczema and easy bruising. Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to infection?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent parathyroid glands with resulting hypocalcemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of the blood-thymus barrier allowing antigen entry

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstruction of the superior vena cava by a thymic mass

explanation.summary: In Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, the recurrent infections are due to a hypoplastic or aplastic thymus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by abnormalities of the WAS gene, producing a triad of recurrent infections due to a hypoplastic or aplastic thymus, eczema, and thrombocytopenia with small platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Parathyroid hypoplasia with hypocalcemia is a feature of DiGeorge syndrome, not Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuromuscular junction autoantibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which produces weakness rather than infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Breaching the blood-thymus barrier would disrupt T cell selection but is not the mechanism in this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superior vena cava obstruction is a complication of mediastinal neoplasms and does not cause recurrent infection.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A surgeon performs a median sternotomy to remove the thymus. Immediately after the sternum is divided, where should the thymus be found?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the left pleural space, at the hilum of the lung

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the neck, superior to the thyroid gland and larynx

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the posterior mediastinum, behind the esophagus and aorta

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the superior mediastinum, in front of the heart and great vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the pericardial sac, on the anterior surface of the heart

explanation.summary: The thymus lies in the anterior part of the superior mediastinum, behind the sternum and in front of the heart and great vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus is a bilobed, encapsulated organ located in the anterior part of the superior mediastinum. It lies behind the sternum, in front of the heart and great vessels, and between the lungs. It is roughly midline but may be offset to either side of the thorax as a normal variant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The thymus lies between the lungs in the midline region, not within a pleural space at the hilum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The thymus is an upper thoracic organ, inferior to the thyroid gland rather than above it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The thymus sits anteriorly, not behind the esophagus and aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus lies in front of the heart but outside the pericardial sac.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A child with severe thymic hypoplasia mounts poor antibody responses to vaccination even though circulating B cells are present in normal numbers. Which of the following functions of mature T cells best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They form the net-like scaffolding of the blood-thymus barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: They potentiate B cells to secrete antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: They present self-antigen to thymocytes during negative selection

choices.label: D
choices.text: They regulate the basal metabolic rate of peripheral tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: They remove aged and damaged erythrocytes from the circulation

explanation.summary: One of the functions of mature T cells is potentiating B cells to secrete antibodies, so a failed thymus impairs antibody responses even when B cells are present.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mature T cells serve many functions, including secreting cytokines, potentiating B cells to secrete antibodies, killing pathogens, and forming immunologic memory. Without adequate thymic output of mature T cells, B cells receive inadequate help and antibody responses are poor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The scaffolding of the blood-thymus barrier is formed by epithelial-reticular cells, not by mature T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antigen presentation during negative selection is carried out by epithelial-reticular cells, B cells, and dendritic cells within the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Regulation of the basal metabolic rate is a function of the thyroid gland.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Removal of aged and damaged erythrocytes is a function of the spleen.

questions.topicName: Structure, Function, and Disorders of the Thymus

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man receiving chemotherapy develops acute vomiting that has not responded to his scheduled agents. He is given metoclopramide, which reaches the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the medulla. Blockade of which of the following receptors in the area postrema is primarily responsible for this drug's antiemetic effect?

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide is a D2 dopamine antagonist that works at the area postrema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide's antiemetic action comes into play when it reaches the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema) in the medulla. Blocking D2 dopamine receptors there inhibits stimulation of the vomiting center. It also antagonizes 5-HT3 receptors, which adds to its effect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GABA receptors are not a target of the antiemetic agents described in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine-1 receptors are targeted by antihistamines and are relevant to the vestibular system, not metoclopramide's primary action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M1 muscarinic receptors are blocked by antimuscarinics such as scopolamine, not by metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK1 substance P receptors are blocked by aprepitant, not metoclopramide.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with breast cancer is started on ondansetron before her chemotherapy infusion. In addition to acting on the chemoreceptor trigger zone, this drug reduces nausea by blocking serotonin receptors at which of the following peripheral sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-adrenergic receptors in the cardiac conduction system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Muscarinic receptors of the inner ear vestibular apparatus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotinic receptors at the skeletal neuromuscular junction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sympathetic ganglia in the abdomen and pelvis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vagus nerve terminals in the gastrointestinal tract

explanation.summary: 5-HT3 antagonists block serotonin both centrally and on peripheral vagal terminals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ondansetron, palonosetron, and granisetron are selective 5-HT3 antagonists that block 5-HT3 receptors in the CTZ within the CNS and 5-HT3 receptors on vagus nerve terminals in the peripheral nervous system. Chemotherapy irritates the GI mucosa, causing serotonin release that stimulates these vagal terminals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-adrenergic receptors in the heart are not targeted; the cardiac concern with these drugs is QT prolongation, not receptor blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inner-ear muscarinic receptors are the target of scopolamine, an antimuscarinic, not ondansetron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nicotinic neuromuscular receptors are unrelated to the antiemetic mechanism of ondansetron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sympathetic ganglia are not the site of 5-HT3 antagonist action described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is scheduled for a chemotherapy infusion known to cause a high incidence of emesis. About 30 minutes before the infusion he is given aprepitant to prevent nausea and vomiting. This drug is not effective on an as-needed basis because of which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks the NK1 receptor to prevent substance P binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depletes serotonin stores in the GI mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: It neutralizes chemotherapy drugs in the bloodstream

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates gastric emptying to clear emetogenic drugs

explanation.summary: Aprepitant is an NK1 (substance P) antagonist used as pre-treatment, not as a rescue drug.
