explanation.whyCorrect: Aprepitant crosses the BBB and selectively blocks the NK1 receptor to inhibit binding of substance P, which normally causes pain, nausea, and vomiting. Because of this preventive mechanism it is not effective as needed; it is given as pre-treatment about 30 minutes before the infusion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Depleting serotonin stores is not the mechanism; 5-HT3 antagonists block serotonin receptors rather than deplete stores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aprepitant does not inhibit dopamine synthesis; it acts on NK1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aprepitant does not chemically neutralize chemotherapy drugs in the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increasing gastric emptying describes metoclopramide, not aprepitant.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A patient with chemotherapy-related nausea that has a strong vestibular component is prescribed scopolamine delivered by a transdermal patch. This agent relieves nausea primarily by blocking which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Scopolamine is a nonspecific muscarinic antagonist acting at the M1 receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vestibular system communicates with the nucleus tractus solitarius to induce nausea and vomiting. Scopolamine, an antimuscarinic, crosses the BBB and blocks the M1 receptor to treat motion sickness and can help with chemotherapy-induced nausea. A transdermal patch helps avoid anticholinergic side effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5-HT3 receptors are blocked by ondansetron and related agents, not scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-adrenergic receptors are not involved in scopolamine's antiemetic action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D2 dopamine receptors are the target of metoclopramide, not scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK1 receptors are the target of aprepitant, not scopolamine.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman receives dexamethasone as part of her pre-treatment regimen before a highly emetogenic chemotherapy infusion. During therapy she is monitored for which of the following adverse effects most commonly associated with corticosteroid use in this setting?

explanation.summary: In chemotherapy-induced nausea, steroids most commonly cause hyperglycemia and GI bleed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are used as pre-treatment for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Although steroids can have many side effects, when used in this setting the most common are hyperglycemia and risk of GI bleed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutropenia is listed as an uncommon effect of aprepitant, not steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pupillary dilation is an anticholinergic effect of scopolamine, not steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: QT-interval prolongation is a rare effect of 5-HT3 antagonists, not corticosteroids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tardive dyskinesia is a serious CNS effect of metoclopramide, not steroids.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man who has taken metoclopramide for several months for chronic nausea develops involuntary, repetitive movements of his tongue and lips that do not resolve when the drug is stopped. This adverse effect is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Chronic metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia, which is often irreversible.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide can cause severe CNS adverse effects, including extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia, which is often irreversible. The persistent involuntary orofacial movements after stopping the drug fit tardive dyskinesia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperglycemia is a steroid effect and does not cause involuntary movements.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutropenia is an uncommon effect of aprepitant, not a cause of involuntary movements.
whyWrongByChoice.C: QT-interval prolongation is a 5-HT3 antagonist effect and is a cardiac finding, not a movement disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serotonin syndrome is a risk when metoclopramide is combined with SSRIs, but it presents acutely with autonomic and neuromuscular changes, not persistent orofacial dyskinesia.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for depression is being considered for an antiemetic. The team notes that adding one particular agent could precipitate serotonin syndrome, especially in young adults and at high doses. Which of the following drugs is being avoided for this reason?

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide should not be combined with SSRIs due to serotonin syndrome risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states metoclopramide should not be used with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors because of the risk of serotonin syndrome, particularly in children and young adults and at high doses. This reflects metoclopramide's activity at 5-HT3 receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant is an NK1 antagonist and is not linked to serotonin syndrome with SSRIs in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid and is not associated with serotonin syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone is a corticosteroid, not a serotonergic drug, and does not carry this caution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scopolamine is an antimuscarinic and does not carry this serotonin syndrome caution.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who recently gave birth is struggling to produce breast milk. Her physician notes that one antiemetic increases prolactin secretion and could be used to stimulate lactation, though it is not often used for this purpose because of its other adverse effects. Which of the following best explains how this drug increases milk production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the gut, increasing prolactin release

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks dopamine, relieving dopamine's inhibition of prolactin secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks NK1 receptors centrally, raising substance P and prolactin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It directly stimulates prolactin receptors in the breast alveolar cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suppresses circulating inflammatory mediators that inhibit milk letdown

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide raises prolactin because dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide can increase milk production in both males and females. Dopamine naturally inhibits secretion of prolactin, the hormone responsible for milk production; by blocking dopamine, metoclopramide relieves this inhibition and prolactin rises.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lactation effect is due to dopamine blockade, not 5-HT3 receptor activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking NK1 receptors describes aprepitant and is unrelated to prolactin secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metoclopramide does not directly stimulate breast prolactin receptors; it acts by removing dopamine's inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppressing inflammatory mediators describes the antiemetic mechanism of steroids, not the prolactin effect.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A patient on ondansetron for chemotherapy-induced nausea is monitored with periodic electrocardiograms. Which of the following is the major, though rare, adverse effect that prompts this monitoring?

explanation.summary: The major but rare adverse effect of 5-HT3 antagonists is QT-interval prolongation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several adverse effects of the serotonin antagonists include headache, dizziness, and constipation. A major side effect to look out for is prolongation of the QT interval, but this is rare, which is why an ECG may be monitored.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperglycemia is a corticosteroid effect, not a 5-HT3 antagonist effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a severe CNS effect of metoclopramide, not ondansetron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pupillary dilation is an anticholinergic effect of scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tardive dyskinesia is a metoclopramide effect, not an ondansetron effect.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man is about to begin cisplatin, which carries the highest emesis risk of the chemotherapy drugs with an incidence greater than 90%. Following the preferred multi-drug approach, which of the following three-drug antiemetic regimens is most appropriate as a starting point?

explanation.summary: High-emesis-risk cisplatin warrants at least a three-drug regimen of aprepitant, ondansetron, and dexamethasone.
explanation.whyCorrect: A multi-drug regimen is preferred to prevent stimuli from multiple sources. A patient receiving cisplatin (highest emesis risk, incidence >90%) would receive at least a three-drug antiemetic regimen that includes aprepitant, ondansetron, and dexamethasone. Other agents like an antimuscarinic or D2 antagonist may be added if needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Scopolamine is an add-on for vestibular symptoms; the base triple therapy pairs a steroid and 5-HT3 antagonist with an NK1 antagonist, not scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This combination lacks a 5-HT3 antagonist and a steroid, which are core components of the recommended regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This combination lacks the NK1 antagonist and steroid; scopolamine and metoclopramide are add-ons if needed, not the base regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This regimen omits the recommended NK1 antagonist and 5-HT3 antagonist that anchor the standard cisplatin regimen.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with breast cancer on ongoing chemotherapy reports persistent nausea despite consistent use of ondansetron. Her team wants to add a second agent with a different mechanism for her breakthrough nausea. Because the NK1 antagonist and steroid are used mainly as pre-treatment and an antimuscarinic is best for motion sickness, which of the following is the most appropriate addition?

explanation.summary: For breakthrough nausea in a patient already on a 5-HT3 antagonist, a D2 antagonist is the best add-on.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient already takes ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist. NK1 antagonists (aprepitant) and steroids (dexamethasone) are used primarily as pre-treatment before infusions, and antimuscarinics (scopolamine) are most helpful for motion sickness. D2 antagonists are reserved for breakthrough nausea, so metoclopramide is the best option to add.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant is used primarily as pre-treatment before the infusion and is not effective on an as-needed basis for breakthrough symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dexamethasone is used mainly as pre-treatment, not as an add-on for breakthrough nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Palonosetron is another 5-HT3 antagonist and shares ondansetron's mechanism, so it would not add a different mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scopolamine is most helpful for vestibular/motion sickness, which is not the driver of this patient's nausea.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: During chemotherapy, irritation of the GI mucosa leads to release of a mediator that acts on receptors located in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and on vagal terminals to increase motility and provoke nausea. Which of the following mediators is chiefly responsible?

explanation.summary: Chemotherapy-induced GI irritation causes mucosal serotonin release that drives nausea via 5-HT3 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chemotherapy can cause GI irritation, which in turn causes mucosal secretion of serotonin in the GI tract; this increases motility and leads to nausea. Serotonin acts on 5-HT3 receptors in the CTZ and on vagal terminals, which is why 5-HT3 antagonists are effective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine acts at muscarinic receptors and is targeted by antimuscarinics, but it is not the mediator released from irritated GI mucosa here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dopamine acts at D2 receptors in the area postrema; it is not the mediator released from the irritated GI mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine acts at H1 receptors relevant to the vestibular system, not the mucosal serotonin release described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Substance P acts at NK1 receptors and is blocked by aprepitant, but it is not the GI-mucosal mediator described.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman becomes nauseated whenever she turns her head during a car ride. Signals from her vestibular apparatus travel to a structure in the medulla that functions as the vomiting center. Which of the following structures is this?

explanation.summary: The vomiting center is the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vestibular system communicates with the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla to induce nausea and vomiting. This nucleus is the vomiting center and carries H1, M1, NK1, and 5-HT3 receptors that antiemetics can target.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The area postrema is the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which senses circulating stimuli; it is not itself the vomiting center.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cortex is a higher CNS input to emesis, not the medullary vomiting center.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fourth ventricle is an anatomic landmark adjacent to these nuclei, not the vomiting center.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hypothalamus is one of the central nervous system sites that can feed into emesis, but it is not the medullary vomiting center.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man receiving chemotherapy notes that his nausea is markedly worse when he stands up or rolls over in bed, suggesting a vestibular contribution. Which pair of receptors mediates signaling from the vestibular system in the pathway to the vomiting center?

explanation.summary: The vestibular system signals through histamine-1 and M1 muscarinic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the emesis pathway, the vestibular system carries histamine-1 and M1 receptors and communicates with the nucleus tractus solitarius. This is why an antimuscarinic such as scopolamine, which blocks the M1 receptor, is the agent used for vestibular nausea and motion sickness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NK1 and 5-HT3 receptors are targets of aprepitant and ondansetron, which are not the agents used for vestibular nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M1 is correct for the vestibular system, but D2 is an area postrema receptor rather than a vestibular one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: D2 and NK1 receptors are chemoreceptor trigger zone receptors, not the vestibular pair.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 5-HT3 receptors sit in the CTZ and on peripheral vagal terminals, and D2 receptors in the area postrema; neither is the vestibular pair.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus reports early satiety, bloating, and vomiting of undigested food. He is started on metoclopramide, and his symptoms improve. Which of the following best describes how this drug improves his gastric emptying?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking 5-HT3 receptors on vagal terminals slows intestinal transit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking D2 receptors increases cholinergic stimulation of smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocking M1 receptors relaxes the pyloric sphincter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blocking NK1 receptors prevents substance P-mediated gastric spasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppressing inflammatory mediators reduces gastric mucosal edema

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide's prokinetic effect comes from D2 blockade increasing cholinergic stimulation of gut smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide blocks the D2 receptor, which increases cholinergic stimulation of smooth muscle and increases gastric emptying. This is the basis for its use in patients with diabetic gastroparesis, separate from its antiemetic action at the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5-HT3 blockade is an antiemetic action, and slowing transit would worsen rather than improve gastroparesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M1 blockade describes scopolamine and would reduce, not increase, cholinergic smooth muscle activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK1 blockade describes aprepitant, which is used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and has no prokinetic role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppressing inflammatory mediators is the presumed antiemetic mechanism of corticosteroids, not a prokinetic mechanism.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A patient is to be started on an antiemetic whose major adverse effects include QT prolongation and torsades de pointes as well as extrapyramidal symptoms, mental depression, and tardive dyskinesia. Which of the following agents fits this adverse-effect profile?

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide, the D2 antagonist, combines cardiac conduction risk with severe CNS effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The D2 antagonist metoclopramide is listed with major adverse effects of QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, extrapyramidal symptoms, mental depression, and tardive dyskinesia. No other antiemetic class in this brick carries that combination of cardiac and CNS toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant has limited adverse effects; the uncommon ones are neutropenia and fatigue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dexamethasone in this setting most commonly causes hyperglycemia and risk of GI bleed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone is a corticosteroid with the same steroid adverse-effect profile, not CNS movement disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scopolamine causes pupillary dilation, dry mouth, and sedation, not extrapyramidal symptoms or torsades.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man on high-dose metoclopramide for intractable vomiting is brought in with a temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F), generalized muscular rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability. He takes no antidepressants or other serotonergic drugs. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute dystonic reaction of the neck

explanation.summary: Fever, rigidity, and altered mental status on a D2 antagonist indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is listed among the severe CNS adverse effects of metoclopramide, along with extrapyramidal symptoms, mental depression, tardive dyskinesia, and Parkinsonian features. The triad of hyperthermia, rigidity, and altered mental status in a patient on a D2 antagonist is the classic presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An acute dystonic reaction causes sustained abnormal posturing without hyperthermia or autonomic instability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serotonin syndrome is the risk when metoclopramide is combined with an SSRI, and this patient takes no serotonergic drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tardive dyskinesia produces persistent involuntary movements and is often irreversible, but it does not cause fever or autonomic instability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parkinsonian features involve bradykinesia, tremor, and rigidity without fever or altered mental status.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: Two hours after receiving intravenous metoclopramide, a 22-year-old woman develops an involuntary sustained contraction of her neck muscles pulling her head to one side, along with restlessness. Which of the following adverse effects best describes this presentation?

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide causes restlessness, fatigue, and dystonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide's adverse effects can be severe and include restlessness, fatigue, and dystonia. Sustained involuntary muscle contraction producing abnormal posturing shortly after a dose is a dystonic reaction, part of this drug's extrapyramidal toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Constipation is an adverse effect of the 5-HT3 antagonists, not metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperglycemia is a corticosteroid adverse effect and does not cause muscle contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutropenia is an uncommon adverse effect of aprepitant and is a laboratory abnormality, not a movement disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupillary dilation is an anticholinergic effect of scopolamine.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman who has taken an antiemetic for many months is noted to have bradykinesia, a resting tremor, and cogwheel rigidity. Her medication list includes one agent known to produce Parkinsonian features. Which of the following is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Parkinsonian features are among metoclopramide's severe CNS adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide produces severe CNS adverse effects including extrapyramidal symptoms, mental depression, tardive dyskinesia, Parkinsonian features, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Its dopamine D2 antagonism accounts for the parkinsonism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant has limited adverse effects, with neutropenia and fatigue the uncommon ones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granisetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist and shares ondansetron's profile, which does not include parkinsonism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ondansetron's adverse effects are headache, dizziness, constipation, and rare QT prolongation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scopolamine causes anticholinergic effects such as pupillary dilation, dry mouth, and sedation.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is receiving aprepitant as part of her antiemetic regimen. Although this drug has few adverse effects, the team follows a specific laboratory value regularly while she is on chemotherapy because of one uncommon effect of the drug. Which of the following is being monitored?

explanation.summary: Neutropenia is an uncommon adverse effect of aprepitant and is monitored during chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aprepitant has few adverse effects compared with other antiemetic agents. Among the uncommon ones are neutropenia, which is regularly monitored while the patient is receiving chemotherapy, and fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal function is not the monitored value tied to aprepitant's adverse-effect profile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serum glucose is followed with corticosteroids such as dexamethasone because of hyperglycemia, not with aprepitant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potassium is not among the adverse effects attributed to aprepitant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolactin rises with metoclopramide because dopamine inhibits prolactin secretion; aprepitant does not affect it.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man receiving chemotherapy with aprepitant pre-treatment reports profound fatigue. His oncologist notes that although fatigue is listed among the drug's adverse effects, attributing it to aprepitant alone would be premature. Which of the following best explains this reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aprepitant does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so central effects are unlikely

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatigue from aprepitant is an early sign of QT prolongation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fatigue from aprepitant occurs only when it is dosed as needed rather than as pre-treatment before chemotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fatigue from aprepitant reflects unrecognized hyperglycemia from the regimen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fatigue may be closely associated with the chemotherapy the patient is receiving

explanation.summary: Fatigue in a patient on aprepitant is confounded by the chemotherapy itself.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aprepitant's uncommon adverse effects include neutropenia and fatigue, but the fatigue may also be closely associated with the chemotherapy the patient is receiving. Attribution therefore requires accounting for the underlying regimen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant does cross the blood-brain barrier to block NK1 receptors centrally.
whyWrongByChoice.B: QT prolongation is the rare cardiac effect of 5-HT3 antagonists and is not signaled by fatigue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aprepitant is not effective on an as-needed basis at all; it is given as pre-treatment, and its adverse effects are not dosing-schedule specific in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperglycemia is a corticosteroid effect and is not the stated explanation for aprepitant-associated fatigue.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman receives aprepitant before a chemotherapy infusion. The drug crosses the blood-brain barrier and prevents a neuropeptide from binding its receptor. Which set of effects is normally produced by that neuropeptide?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperglycemia, GI bleeding, and fluid retention

explanation.summary: Substance P, blocked at NK1 receptors by aprepitant, normally causes pain, nausea, and vomiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aprepitant crosses the blood-brain barrier and selectively blocks the NK1 receptor to inhibit binding of substance P, which normally causes pain, nausea, and vomiting. Preventing that binding is how the drug prevents chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Constipation, diarrhea, and headache are adverse effects of the 5-HT3 antagonists, not actions of substance P.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperglycemia and GI bleeding are corticosteroid adverse effects, not substance P actions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Restlessness, dystonia, and depression are adverse effects of metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertigo, dry mouth, and sedation relate to vestibular nausea and anticholinergic effects of scopolamine.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A resident is asked to select a selective 5-HT3 antagonist from a patient's formulary list. Which of the following drugs belongs to that class?

explanation.summary: Ondansetron, palonosetron, and granisetron are the selective 5-HT3 antagonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ondansetron, palonosetron, and granisetron are selective 5-HT3 antagonists that block 5-HT3 receptors in the CTZ and on vagus nerve terminals. The shared -setron stem marks the class.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant is a neurokinin 1 receptor antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid used as pre-treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist; it has some 5-HT3 activity but is not a selective 5-HT3 antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scopolamine is a nonspecific muscarinic antagonist acting at the M1 receptor.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman is starting granisetron for prophylaxis before chemotherapy. She asks what bothersome symptoms she should expect. Which of the following is a common adverse effect of this drug class?

explanation.summary: Headache, dizziness, and constipation are the common adverse effects of 5-HT3 antagonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several adverse effects of the serotonin antagonists include headache, dizziness, and constipation; the class is also associated with diarrhea. These are the everyday complaints, in contrast to the rare but major QT prolongation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dystonia is an extrapyramidal effect of metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperglycemia is a corticosteroid adverse effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutropenia is an uncommon adverse effect of aprepitant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupillary dilation is an anticholinergic effect of scopolamine.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man on moderately emetogenic chemotherapy has been given both aprepitant and ondansetron. He asks why he may take one of them at home when he feels sick but not the other. Which of the following best explains the difference between these two agents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aprepitant both treats and prevents chemotherapy nausea, whereas ondansetron is prophylaxis only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aprepitant must be dosed after the infusion, whereas ondansetron must be dosed well before it

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both drugs act on the same receptor, but only ondansetron reaches the chemoreceptor trigger zone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ondansetron both treats and prevents chemotherapy nausea, whereas aprepitant is pre-treatment only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ondansetron requires regular monitoring of the neutrophil count, which limits at-home dosing

explanation.summary: 5-HT3 antagonists treat and prevent CINV; aprepitant is a pre-treatment drug only.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ondansetron and the other 5-HT3 antagonists are indicated for treatment of nausea related to cancer chemotherapy and are also recommended for prophylaxis against chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Aprepitant, because its mechanism is to prevent substance P binding, is not effective on an as-needed basis and is given as pre-treatment about 30 minutes before the infusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the two drugs; aprepitant is the one that cannot be used as needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aprepitant is given roughly 30 minutes before the infusion, not after it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They act on different receptors: aprepitant at NK1 and ondansetron at 5-HT3, and both reach central sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia monitoring belongs to aprepitant, not ondansetron, and is not the reason for the dosing difference.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chemotherapy-related nausea and a vestibular component is to receive scopolamine. His physician chooses a transdermal patch rather than oral dosing. Which of the following is the best rationale for this route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts the drug from a nonspecific to a selective M1 antagonist

choices.label: B
choices.text: It eliminates the risk of QT-interval prolongation seen with oral dosing

choices.label: C
choices.text: It permits rapid as-needed dosing during episodes of acute vomiting

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents the drug from crossing the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reduces anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and sedation

explanation.summary: A transdermal patch is used to limit scopolamine's anticholinergic adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: All anticholinergics carry major adverse effects of pupillary dilation, dry mouth, and possible sedation. These side effects are best avoided by using a transdermal patch, which is why scopolamine is commonly delivered this way.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Scopolamine remains a nonspecific muscarinic antagonist regardless of the route used.
whyWrongByChoice.B: QT prolongation is a rare effect of the 5-HT3 antagonists, not of scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A patch provides steady delivery rather than the rapid onset needed for acute as-needed dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine must cross the blood-brain barrier to block the central M1 receptor; the patch does not prevent that.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man wearing a scopolamine patch is brought to the emergency department with warm flushed skin, a dry mouth, urinary retention, and confusion. Which additional physical finding is most consistent with this toxicity?

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinic toxicity produces mydriasis along with dry, flushed skin, retention, and confusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: All anticholinergics produce pupillary dilation, dry mouth, and possible sedation, and the classic antimuscarinic picture is blurry vision, overheating, dry mouth, flushed skin, urinary retention, and confusion. Dilated pupils complete this toxidrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Muscarinic blockade relaxes airway smooth muscle rather than producing bronchospasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dry mouth, not excessive salivation, is the expected secretory effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pinpoint pupils are the opposite of the pupillary dilation that muscarinic blockade produces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic blockade causes dry skin and overheating rather than sweating.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: Four patients on chemotherapy report nausea with different features. For which of the following patients is scopolamine the most appropriate agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A patient needing pre-treatment 30 minutes before a highly emetogenic infusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: A patient needing serotonin blockade at vagal terminals in the gut

choices.label: C
choices.text: A patient with acute vomiting who also has diabetic gastroparesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: A patient with hyperglycemia who needs prophylaxis before an infusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: A patient with vertigo whose symptoms worsen with head motion

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinics such as scopolamine are best for vestibular nausea and vertigo.
explanation.whyCorrect: Scopolamine blocks the M1 receptor to treat vertigo and motion sickness and is the agent for vestibular nausea, though it can also be helpful in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Nausea that worsens with head motion points to the vestibular pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pre-treatment before a highly emetogenic infusion calls for aprepitant, an NK1 antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serotonin blockade at vagal terminals is the action of a 5-HT3 antagonist, not an antimuscarinic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute vomiting with gastroparesis calls for metoclopramide, which also increases gastric emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prophylaxis with a 5-HT3 antagonist is appropriate here, and the steroid component would be the concern for hyperglycemia; scopolamine addresses neither.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman receives dexamethasone with her antiemetic regimen. A student asks how corticosteroids reduce chemotherapy-induced nausea. Which of the following is the proposed mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of 5-HT3 receptors on peripheral vagal nerve terminals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of the M1 muscarinic receptor in the vestibular pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: Competitive blockade of D2 receptors in the area postrema of the medulla

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selective blockade of NK1 receptors to inhibit substance P signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of the release of inflammatory mediators in the bloodstream

explanation.summary: Steroids are thought to work by suppressing inflammatory mediators that contribute to nausea.
explanation.whyCorrect: The exact mechanism of the antiemetic properties of corticosteroids is unknown, but it is thought that they suppress the release of inflammatory mediators in the bloodstream that contribute to nausea. They are combined with other antiemetics as pre-treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5-HT3 blockade at vagal terminals is the mechanism of ondansetron and related agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M1 blockade in the vestibular pathway is the mechanism of scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D2 blockade in the area postrema is the mechanism of metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK1 blockade to inhibit substance P is the mechanism of aprepitant.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A patient's antiemetic regimen calls for a corticosteroid before her infusion, but dexamethasone is unavailable. Which of the following is an appropriate alternative from the same class?

explanation.summary: Dexamethasone, methylprednisone, and prednisone are the corticosteroids commonly used as antiemetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids are combined with other antiemetics as pre-treatment for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and dexamethasone, methylprednisone, and prednisone are the agents most commonly used. Methylprednisone therefore substitutes within the same class.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant is an NK1 antagonist, a different class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granisetron is another 5-HT3 antagonist, not a steroid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist, a different class.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scopolamine is an antimuscarinic, not a steroid.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man receiving dexamethasone as antiemetic pre-treatment, who also takes a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for bone pain, develops epigastric pain and passes black tarry stools. Which of the following adverse effects of his antiemetic regimen best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: When used for CINV, steroids most commonly cause hyperglycemia and GI bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Steroids have many possible side effects, but when used for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting the most common are hyperglycemia and risk of GI bleed. Epigastric pain with melena in a patient on a steroid plus an NSAID reflects that bleeding risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutropenia is an uncommon aprepitant effect and would not produce melena.
whyWrongByChoice.C: QT prolongation is a rare 5-HT3 antagonist effect and is a cardiac finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tardive dyskinesia is a metoclopramide effect and causes involuntary movements, not GI bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary retention is part of the anticholinergic profile of scopolamine.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: An oncologist is planning antiemetic prophylaxis and stratifies the planned chemotherapy by emesis risk. Which of the following agents is categorized as high risk for emesis?

explanation.summary: Cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin are high-risk emetogenic chemotherapy drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chemotherapy drugs are categorized as high risk for emesis (for example cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin), moderate risk, or low risk. High-risk agents demand the most aggressive multi-drug antiemetic prophylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Most targeted monoclonal antibodies are in the low-risk category.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aprepitant is an antiemetic given as pre-treatment, not a chemotherapy drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dexamethasone is an antiemetic corticosteroid, not a chemotherapy drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ondansetron is an antiemetic, not a chemotherapy agent to be stratified by emesis risk.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman beginning highly emetogenic chemotherapy is prescribed three antiemetics with different mechanisms rather than a higher dose of a single agent. Which of the following is the best rationale for this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combination therapy converts the chemotherapy from high emesis risk to low emesis risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combining agents allows each drug to be given at a lower frequency than as monotherapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each additional agent blocks a different subtype of the D2 receptor in the area postrema

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emetic stimuli arise from multiple sources and receptors, so several targets must be covered

choices.label: E
choices.text: Giving several agents prevents the neutropenia expected with single-agent therapy

explanation.summary: Multi-drug antiemetic regimens are preferred because emetic stimuli come from multiple sources.
explanation.whyCorrect: A multi-drug regimen is preferred for antiemetics to prevent stimuli from multiple sources. The CTZ alone contains D2, 5-HT3, histamine-1, and neurokinin-1 receptors, and additional receptors are located throughout the body, so blocking a single receptor leaves other pathways open.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Combination therapy manages symptoms; it does not change the emetogenic risk category of the chemotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dosing frequency is not the stated reason for combining antiemetics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The agents act on different receptor families, not on different subtypes of D2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia is an uncommon adverse effect of aprepitant and is not prevented by combining antiemetics.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed metastatic cancer reports persistent nausea, but he has not yet started any chemotherapy and takes no medications. Which of the following best accounts for his symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of D2 receptors in the area postrema

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflammatory mediator suppression that has been withdrawn

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serotonin release from gastrointestinal mucosa irritated by cytotoxic cancer drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cancer itself acting as a stimulus at the chemoreceptor trigger zone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vestibular stimulation of the nucleus tractus solitarius by tumor burden

explanation.summary: Cancer itself can stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone, even before chemotherapy begins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nausea and vomiting are commonly encountered in cancer patients. The cancer itself can be a stimulus within the chemoreceptor trigger zone, although more often it is the chemotherapy drugs that induce receptors within the CTZ to cause nausea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: D2 blockade in the area postrema is an antiemetic drug action, not a cause of nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Steroid suppression of inflammatory mediators is a treatment mechanism; he is on no medications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chemotherapy-induced GI irritation with mucosal serotonin release requires cytotoxic drugs, which he has not received.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vestibular input drives motion-related nausea and is not the described mechanism for tumor-associated nausea.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: During chemotherapy, chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the gastrointestinal tract and heart send afferent signals to the medullary vomiting center. Which of the following cranial nerves carry these afferents?

explanation.summary: Peripheral emetic afferents from the gut and heart travel in cranial nerves IX and X.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors of the gastrointestinal tract and heart, which carry 5-HT3 receptors, project to the vomiting center by way of cranial nerve IX or X. This is the peripheral pathway that 5-HT3 antagonists interrupt at vagal terminals.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The hypoglossal and accessory nerves are motor nerves to the tongue and neck muscles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The oculomotor and trochlear nerves supply extraocular muscles and have no role in emesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The trigeminal and facial nerves do not carry visceral afferents from the gut and heart to the vomiting center.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vestibulocochlear nerve serves the vestibular pathway, which is a separate input, and the facial nerve is not involved.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man receiving cisplatin has been pre-treated with aprepitant, ondansetron, and dexamethasone. He still reports nausea, and it reliably appears when he sits up or turns his head, with an accompanying sense of the room spinning. Which of the following should be added?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A second dose of aprepitant as needed

explanation.summary: Vestibular symptoms on top of a three-drug regimen call for adding an antimuscarinic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three-drug regimen of aprepitant, ondansetron, and dexamethasone is a starting point, and other medications such as an antimuscarinic or a D2 antagonist may be added if needed. Nausea provoked by head movement with vertigo is vestibular, and scopolamine blocks the M1 receptor to treat vertigo.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant is not effective on an as-needed basis because it acts by preventing substance P binding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metoclopramide is the add-on for breakthrough or acute vomiting rather than for symptoms with a clear vestibular trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Palonosetron is another 5-HT3 antagonist and would duplicate the mechanism of the ondansetron he already receives.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone is a corticosteroid and would duplicate the dexamethasone already in his regimen.

questions.topicName: Supportive Therapy for Patients on Chemotherapy - Antiemetics

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman returns from a trip to sub-Saharan Africa with high recurring fevers, chills, and myalgia. She now has altered consciousness and a seizure. A Giemsa-stained blood smear shows numerous ring-form trophozoites within red blood cells and a crescent (banana)-shaped gametocyte. Which species of Plasmodium is the most likely cause of her illness?

explanation.summary: Crescent-shaped gametocytes and severe (cerebral) malaria point to P. falciparum.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. falciparum is the most common and deadliest species. Its gametocytes have a distinct crescent (banana) shape, unlike the round gametocytes of other species. It is the species most associated with severe complications such as cerebral malaria, which causes coma and seizures.

whyWrongByChoice.B: P. knowlesi is a primate parasite responsible for only a small number of cases and does not have crescent-shaped gametocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. malariae has round gametocytes and causes a quartan fever without the crescent gametocyte or cerebral malaria described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. ovale has round gametocytes and typically causes a milder, relapsing course.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P. vivax gametocytes are round rather than crescent-shaped, and it more often causes relapsing rather than severe cerebral disease.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who recently traveled to an endemic region develops fever and chills that recur in a regular pattern precisely every 72 hours. A blood smear confirms malaria. Which species of Plasmodium is most consistent with this quartan fever pattern?

explanation.summary: A fever recurring every 72 hours (quartan fever) is characteristic of P. malariae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because different species have different maturation times within RBCs, the interval between fevers varies by species. P. malariae causes a quartan fever, which occurs every 72 hours as the synchronized parasites rupture RBCs in waves.

whyWrongByChoice.A: P. falciparum initially causes quotidian fever (every 24 hours), later becoming tertian (every 48 hours), not quartan.
whyWrongByChoice.B: P. knowlesi causes quotidian fever every 24 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. ovale causes tertian fever every 48 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P. vivax causes tertian fever every 48 hours.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is successfully treated for malaria after a trip abroad. Eight months later, having not traveled since, he develops a new episode of malaria with a fever recurring every 48 hours. Which of the following best explains this relapse so long after the initial infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dormant hypnozoites persisted in the liver and reactivated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gametocytes remained circulating in the bloodstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sporozoites remained latent in the skin at the bite site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trophozoites entered a prolonged ring-form state in RBCs

explanation.summary: Relapse of malaria months to years later is caused by dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale.
explanation.whyCorrect: In P. vivax and P. ovale, parasites can reside in the liver in a dormant form called a hypnozoite for days, weeks, or even years. These hypnozoites can eventually reactivate and cause relapse of disease long after the initial infection. The 48-hour (tertian) fever fits P. vivax or P. ovale.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gametocytes are the sexual form taken up by mosquitoes and fall out of the replication cycle; they do not cause a later relapse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick does not describe merozoites hiding in splenic macrophages to cause relapse; the dormant reservoir is the liver hypnozoite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sporozoites travel from the skin to the liver soon after the bite; they do not remain latent in the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A prolonged ring-form trophozoite state in RBCs is not the mechanism of relapse; dormancy occurs in the liver as a hypnozoite.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A researcher notes that individuals from certain West African populations whose red blood cells lack a particular surface receptor are essentially resistant to infection by Plasmodium vivax. Absence of which of the following provides this complete protection?

explanation.summary: P. vivax uses the Duffy antigen to enter RBCs, so its absence prevents infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. vivax uses the Duffy antigen to enter red blood cells. Absence of the Duffy antigen therefore prevents P. vivax from invading the RBC, providing complete protection against this species.

whyWrongByChoice.B: G6PD deficiency provides partial protection by making infected RBCs prone to oxidative damage, not by blocking a receptor P. vivax needs to enter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin S (as in sickle cell trait) makes RBCs less hospitable to the parasite but does not act as the entry receptor for P. vivax.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PfEMP1 is an adhesion molecule expressed by P. falciparum-infected RBCs that binds endothelium; it is not the RBC receptor used by P. vivax.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein and is not described as the entry receptor for P. vivax.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A hematologist explains that a patient with sickle cell trait (HbAS) has some natural protection against severe malaria. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The abnormal hemoglobin makes red blood cells less hospitable to the parasite

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trait blocks invasion of hepatocytes by circulating sporozoites

choices.label: C
choices.text: The trait eliminates the Duffy antigen required for parasite entry into cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The trait prevents female mosquitoes from transmitting the parasite

choices.label: E
choices.text: The trait produces antibodies that neutralize circulating merozoites

explanation.summary: Abnormal hemoglobin in sickle cell trait makes RBCs less hospitable to Plasmodium.
explanation.whyCorrect: In sickle cell trait, one abnormal allele is paired with a normal allele (HbAS), a phenotype that is protective against malaria without causing severe sickle cell disease. The abnormal hemoglobin makes RBCs less hospitable to Plasmodium spp., leading to protection against severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The protection operates in the RBC stage via abnormal hemoglobin, not by blocking sporozoite invasion of hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of the Duffy antigen is a separate mechanism specific to P. vivax; sickle cell trait works through abnormal hemoglobin, not Duffy antigen loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sickle cell trait affects the red blood cell environment, not mosquito transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes protection to the abnormal hemoglobin's effect on the RBC, not to antibody production against merozoites.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A student is tracing the human stage of the Plasmodium life cycle. After an infected Anopheles mosquito bites a person, which form of the parasite is injected and first travels through the bloodstream to invade hepatocytes?

explanation.summary: Sporozoites are injected by the mosquito and travel to the liver to infect hepatocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasmodium gametocytes within a mosquito develop into sporozoites, the infectious form. During a bite, sporozoites are injected into the human, travel through the bloodstream to the liver, and enter hepatocytes, where they multiply as schizonts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gametocytes are the sexual form taken up by mosquitoes; they do not invade hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Merozoites are released from ruptured liver schizonts into the blood and invade RBCs; they are not the form injected by the mosquito.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ookinete is a mosquito-stage form and is not the form injected into humans to infect the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trophozoites are the active amoeboid form inside red blood cells, not the form that first enters hepatocytes.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected malaria has a complete blood count showing a normocytic/normochromic anemia and an elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase. To confirm the diagnosis and identify the species and parasite burden, which of the following is the gold standard test?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four-fold rise in antibody titers two weeks apart

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measurement of serum bilirubin and haptoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microscopy of a Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid antigen test using monoclonal antibodies

explanation.summary: The gold standard for diagnosing malaria is microscopy of a Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gold standard diagnostic test for malaria is microscopy of a Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear. Smear examination reveals not only the presence of Plasmodium organisms but also the species and the level of parasite burden. The most commonly seen form is the ring-form trophozoite.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood culture is used to diagnose brucellosis, not malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A four-fold rise in antibody titers is a diagnostic approach for brucellosis, not the gold standard for malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bilirubin and haptoglobin reflect hemolysis but do not identify the parasite, species, or burden the way the blood smear does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rapid diagnostic tests using monoclonal antibodies are used when microscopy is not available, especially in resource-limited areas, but they are not the gold standard.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A global health team is deploying the RTS,S malaria vaccine, now recommended for young children in areas endemic for P. falciparum. This vaccine is a virus-like particle made of a fusion protein consisting of hepatitis B surface antigen and which of the following P. falciparum components?

explanation.summary: The RTS,S vaccine combines the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein with hepatitis B surface antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The only malaria vaccine (RTS,S) is recommended for young children in areas endemic for P. falciparum and has about 30% efficacy in reducing severe disease. It is a virus-like particle made of a fusion protein consisting of the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein and hepatitis B surface antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Duffy-binding protein relates to P. vivax RBC entry and is not the component of the RTS,S vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The vaccine uses the circumsporozoite protein, not a gametocyte antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no merozoite surface hemoglobinase component in the RTS,S vaccine described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PfEMP1 is an adhesion molecule expressed on infected RBCs, not the antigen used in the RTS,S vaccine.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man from Connecticut presents with fever, chills, and fatigue several weeks after a summer hiking trip. Laboratory studies reveal hemolytic anemia, and a Giemsa-stained thin blood smear shows intra-erythrocytic parasites arranged as tetrads resembling a Maltese cross. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Maltese cross tetrads in RBCs after a tick-exposure region point to babesiosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In babesiosis, the merozoites are distinct in that they form tetrads that look like a Maltese cross within red blood cells. Combined with tick exposure in the northeastern US and hemolytic anemia, this is characteristic of infection with Babesia spp.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) shares the Ixodes vector but does not form Maltese cross tetrads within red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Brucellosis is caused by gram-negative coccobacilli linked to livestock exposure and does not produce intra-erythrocytic Maltese cross forms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lyme disease is caused by B. burgdorferi and does not appear as intra-RBC tetrads on a blood smear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Malaria parasites form ring-form trophozoites, not Maltese cross tetrads, and are transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, not ticks in Connecticut.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man who underwent a splenectomy years ago is bitten by a tick and develops high fever, severe hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly from Babesia infection. Which of the following features of this patient most increases his risk for severe babesiosis?

explanation.summary: Severe babesiosis occurs mainly in immunosuppressed, asplenic, or elderly patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most patients with babesiosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited flu-like symptoms. Severe clinical disease, with high fever, severe hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly, occurs mainly in patients who are immunosuppressed, asplenic, or elderly. This patient is both asplenic and elderly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absence of the Duffy antigen protects against P. vivax malaria and is not a risk factor for severe babesiosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency provides partial protection against malaria and is not the described risk factor for severe babesiosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Babesiosis is acquired from local Ixodes tick bites in endemic US regions; international travel is not the relevant risk factor here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell trait is protective against severe malaria and is not identified as a risk factor for severe babesiosis.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old veterinarian presents with 3 weeks of recurrent, wave-like fevers, drenching night sweats, malaise, and back pain. Physical exam reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Blood cultures grow small, gram-negative coccobacilli, and she reports frequently handling animals and consuming unpasteurized cheese. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Undulating fever with livestock/unpasteurized-dairy exposure and gram-negative coccobacilli indicates Brucella.
explanation.whyCorrect: Brucellosis is caused by small gram-negative coccobacilli found in livestock. Exposure to animals and consumption of unpasteurized dairy are major risk factors. The disease is called undulating fever because fever spikes come in wave-like motions, and B. melitensis (goats/sheep) is the most virulent and most common cause worldwide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Babesia microti is a tick-borne protozoan that infects RBCs and forms Maltese cross tetrads, not gram-negative coccobacilli on culture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Francisella tularensis usually causes ulceroglandular disease after rabbit or tick exposure, not the undulating fever with dairy/livestock exposure described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P. falciparum causes malaria transmitted by mosquitoes with cyclical fevers, not blood cultures growing gram-negative coccobacilli linked to animal exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia pestis (plague) presents with painful lymphadenitis (buboes) and rapid septicemia after flea or rodent exposure, not an indolent undulating fever.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with brucellosis after weeks of undulating fever. The pathogen has spread to the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes, and repeated attempts to clear it are unsuccessful, producing a prolonged chronic illness. Which of the following properties of Brucella spp. best explains this persistent, disseminated infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It forms dormant hypnozoites within hepatocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It invades red blood cells and lyses them in synchronized waves

choices.label: C
choices.text: It produces a crescent-shaped gametocyte that resists clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes a potent LPS that triggers strong phagocyte activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It survives and replicates inside macrophages

explanation.summary: Brucella escapes destruction and replicates within macrophages, spreading through the reticuloendothelial system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once a person is exposed, Brucella spp. are phagocytized by macrophages but escape destruction, survive, and replicate inside them. This conceals the bacteria from the immune system and lets them spread throughout the reticuloendothelial system, so the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes become common sites, causing a prolonged chronic illness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dormant hypnozoites in the liver are a feature of P. vivax and P. ovale malaria, not Brucella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Invading and lysing RBCs in synchronized waves describes Plasmodium and Babesia, not the intracellular macrophage survival of Brucella.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crescent-shaped gametocytes are a feature of P. falciparum, not Brucella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The LPS of Brucella is poorly recognized by pattern recognition receptors, allowing colonization without strong phagocyte activation, the opposite of triggering strong activation.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with confirmed malaria had irregular fever spikes every day during his first week of illness. By the third week, his fever and chills recur predictably every 48 hours. Which of the following best explains the change from irregular to regularly spaced febrile episodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dormant liver hypnozoites reactivate and enter the blood on a fixed schedule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gametocytes accumulate in the bloodstream and are released at regular intervals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infected red blood cells are progressively sequestered within the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: The maturational cycle of the parasites becomes synchronized so RBCs rupture in waves

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient is repeatedly reinfected by additional mosquito bites carrying sporozoites

explanation.summary: Periodic fevers appear once the parasite's maturational cycle becomes synchronized and RBCs rupture in waves.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fever in malaria is driven by excess inflammatory cytokine release associated with the immune response to the parasite. Early in the course, febrile episodes occur at irregular intervals every day. In later stages, the maturational cycle of the parasites becomes synchronized so that RBCs rupture in waves, causing fevers to recur at characteristic intervals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypnozoites are dormant liver forms that cause relapse of disease months to years later, not the spacing of fevers within a single episode.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gametocytes fall out of the infection and replication cycle once they commit to that phase, so they do not drive the cycles of RBC rupture that produce fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenic sequestration of infected cells is not the described basis for the timing of febrile episodes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeated mosquito bites would not produce a fixed 48-hour interval; the regular interval reflects the synchronized maturation time within RBCs.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with Plasmodium ovale malaria. Once the febrile episodes become regularly spaced, at what interval should the fevers be expected to recur?

explanation.summary: P. ovale, like P. vivax, causes tertian fever occurring every 48 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: The interval between fevers varies by species because each species has a different maturation time within RBCs. P. vivax and P. ovale both cause tertian fever, which occurs every 48 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No Plasmodium species is described as producing fever every 12 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 24-hour (quotidian) interval is seen with P. knowlesi and with P. falciparum early in infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 36-hour interval is not a described malarial fever pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 72-hour (quartan) interval is characteristic of P. malariae, not P. ovale.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with severe falciparum malaria develops focal neurologic deficits, and imaging shows areas of cerebral infarction. Which of the following best explains the ischemia and infarction that occur in the brain and kidneys in severe malaria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypnozoites invade and occlude cerebral capillary endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune complexes are deposited within the walls of large arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infected RBCs adhere to endothelial cells and impede blood flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parasite-derived toxins directly lyse capillary endothelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets are massively sequestered within the enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Infected RBCs become adherent to endothelium, impeding blood flow and causing organ ischemia and infarction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infected RBCs are less deformable and are also more likely to adhere to endothelial cells. As a result, blood flow is impeded, causing ischemia or infarction in the brain, kidneys, and other organs. Cerebral malaria, causing coma and seizures, is one of the recognized complications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypnozoites are dormant forms confined to hepatocytes in P. vivax and P. ovale and do not occlude cerebral vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Large-artery immune complex deposition is not a described feature of malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Direct endothelial lysis by a parasite toxin is not the described mechanism; the problem is adhesion of infected RBCs to endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenomegaly in malaria results from chronic antigenic stimulation and does not explain infarction in the brain and kidneys.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man who has lived his entire life in a malaria-endemic region of Africa is found to have a chronically enlarged spleen that extends 6 cm below the costal margin. He is not acutely ill. Which of the following best explains his splenomegaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic antigenic stimulation from residing in an area of endemicity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct invasion of splenic macrophages by injected sporozoites

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis triggered by transfusional iron overload

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of dormant hypnozoites within splenic sinusoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosis of the splenic vein from tissue factor production

explanation.summary: Splenomegaly in malaria is caused by chronic antigenic stimulation in people who live in endemic areas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenomegaly is listed among the complications of malaria and is caused by chronic antigenic stimulation in people who reside in areas of endemicity, where repeated exposure to the parasite continually stimulates the immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sporozoites travel from the bloodstream to hepatocytes; they do not invade splenic macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis from iron overload is not a described cause of splenomegaly in malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypnozoites are dormant forms that reside in the liver, not in the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor production in malaria leads to thrombosis and multiorgan failure in severe acute disease, not to chronic asymptomatic splenic enlargement.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria becomes oliguric, and her serum creatinine rises over 48 hours. Which of the following best accounts for the acute kidney injury seen in malaria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against the Duffy antigen on renal tubular epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct invasion of renal tubular epithelial cells by circulating merozoites

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obstruction of renal tubules by Maltese cross-shaped intracellular tetrads

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of dormant hypnozoites within the renal cortex and medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction of renal blood flow together with immune reactions in the glomerulus

explanation.summary: Malarial acute kidney injury results from reduced renal blood flow plus immune reactions in the glomerulus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute kidney injury is listed among the complications of malaria and is attributed to a reduction of renal blood flow and immune reactions in the glomerulus. Renal failure is also one of the features of severe disease with multiorgan failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Duffy antigen is an RBC surface antigen used by P. vivax for entry; autoantibodies against it are not a described cause of malarial kidney injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Merozoites invade red blood cells, not renal tubular epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maltese cross tetrads are the merozoite form of Babesia spp. within RBCs and are not a cause of renal injury in malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypnozoites are dormant forms restricted to the liver in P. vivax and P. ovale; P. falciparum does not form them at all.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old traveler with severe malaria develops diffuse bleeding from venipuncture sites at the same time that thrombi are found in several organs. Which of the following parasite-related events initiates this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of platelets in the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of circulating gametocytes to pulmonary endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of circulating antithrombin by hepatic schizonts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of hemoglobin-derived pigment into the plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor production with activation of the clotting cascade

explanation.summary: Tissue factor production activates the clotting cascade, producing thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the complications of malaria is tissue factor production with activation of the clotting cascade, leading to thrombosis in multiple organs. This may cause multiorgan failure, including seizures, stroke, respiratory distress, shock, acute kidney injury, acute liver failure, and disseminated intravascular coagulation with diffuse bleeding and clotting throughout the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated platelet destruction in the spleen is not the described trigger for malarial coagulopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gametocytes fall out of the replication cycle and await ingestion by a mosquito; endothelial binding is a property of RBCs carrying mature asexual forms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antithrombin depletion by liver-stage schizonts is not a described mechanism; schizonts rupture to release merozoites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin released from lysed RBCs contributes to anemia and jaundice, not to activation of the clotting cascade.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with malaria has scleral icterus, pallor, and a normocytic anemia. Which of the following best explains her jaundice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilirubin released into the blood from lysed red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased renal excretion of urobilinogen in the urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of infected hepatocytes to conjugate bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatocyte necrosis caused by circulating gametocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstruction of the common bile duct by liver-stage schizonts

explanation.summary: Hemolysis in malaria releases bilirubin from lysed RBCs, producing jaundice alongside anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In any form of malaria, loss of RBCs may lead to anemia and jaundice. Infected RBCs are less deformable and so are more likely to be damaged and lyse, which decreases the RBC count and increases the bilirubin in the blood released from the lysed RBCs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced urobilinogen excretion is not the described basis for jaundice in malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The jaundice is attributed to bilirubin released from lysed RBCs rather than to a conjugation defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gametocytes remain within RBCs awaiting ingestion by a mosquito and are not described as causing hepatocyte necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver-stage schizonts develop inside hepatocytes and rupture to release merozoites; they do not obstruct the biliary tree.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: During the erythrocytic cycle of malaria, merozoites enter red blood cells and transform into trophozoites, the active amoeboid form of the parasite. Which of the following do these intraerythrocytic parasites use as their food source?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin contained within the red blood cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phospholipids of the red blood cell membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma glucose transported across the RBC membrane

explanation.summary: Merozoites that enter RBCs feed on hemoglobin as they develop into trophozoites and then schizonts.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Stage 3 of the life cycle, the erythrocytic cycle, merozoites enter RBCs where they feed on hemoglobin. The parasites transform into trophozoites, the active amoeboid cell form, which mature into schizonts that rupture and release merozoites, continuing the cycle of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatocyte glycogen belongs to the liver stage; in that stage the sporozoites multiply as schizonts rather than feeding on hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenic macrophage iron stores are not accessible to parasites living inside circulating RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RBC membrane phospholipids are not the described food source; the parasite consumes hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma glucose is not identified as the nutrient source for the intraerythrocytic parasite.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency who lives in an endemic region is noted to have partial protection against malaria. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His hemoglobin polymerizes and traps the parasite inside the cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: His hepatocytes resist sporozoite entry, limiting the liver stage

choices.label: C
choices.text: His plasma contains antibodies that opsonize circulating merozoites

choices.label: D
choices.text: His RBCs have lower antioxidant capacity and are prone to oxidative damage

choices.label: E
choices.text: His RBCs lack the surface antigen the parasite uses to enter them

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency lowers RBC antioxidant capacity so infected cells are destroyed more often, limiting parasite replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: In G6PD deficiency, lower antioxidant capacity makes RBCs prone to oxidative damage. Destruction of infected cells therefore occurs more frequently, which limits parasite replication and provides partial protection against malaria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Polymerizing hemoglobin describes the sickle mutation, where abnormal hemoglobin makes RBCs less hospitable to the parasite.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protection from G6PD deficiency operates in the RBC stage, not by blocking sporozoite entry into hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opsonizing antibodies are not the described basis of protection conferred by G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lacking the entry antigen describes absence of the Duffy antigen, which blocks P. vivax specifically and is a different mutation.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how alpha- and beta-thalassemia provide protection against Plasmodium infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They block gametocyte formation within RBCs, halting transmission

choices.label: B
choices.text: They change RBC structure and metabolism, impairing growth and enhancing clearance

choices.label: C
choices.text: They prevent injected sporozoites from ever reaching hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: They raise RBC antioxidant capacity, shielding cells from oxidative damage

choices.label: E
choices.text: They remove the Duffy antigen that P. vivax uses for RBC entry

explanation.summary: Thalassemias alter RBC structure and metabolism, which impairs Plasmodium growth and enhances clearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both alpha- and beta-thalassemia change RBC structure and metabolism. These changes impair Plasmodium growth within the cell and enhance clearance of the parasite, providing partial protection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No listed protective mutation works by preventing gametocyte formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thalassemias act at the level of the RBC; they do not block sporozoites from reaching the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased antioxidant capacity is the opposite of the G6PD mechanism and is not how thalassemias protect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of the Duffy antigen is a separate mutation that gives complete protection against P. vivax only.

questions.topicName: Plasmodium spp., Babesia spp., and Brucella spp.
